ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Physics-Informed Model for Multi-Focal Depth Estimation based on WavePropagation
PROPOSAL: Based on the optics of wave propagation in a camera, formulate a novel physics-informed model that dictates how light behaves when propagating through a scene and interacting with a camera's lens. The model will leverage insights from wave optics to regularize focal stack depth estimation and sharpen up predicted depth maps. Specifically, design a neural network that combines features derived from wave propagation equations, repeated along the focal dimension, with down-sampling and lateral time-gated convolutions that learn spatial patterns across the stack. Use physics-aware ensembling techniques for optimizing model performance on the above-mentioned focal-stack depth datasets, using real-world time-of-flight measurements as supervision to calibrate the inputs.
CONTROLS: Apply the neural network backbone from proposal 1 to compare against a model that uses only frequency-domain features in combination with wave propagation formulation variants.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Focal-Stack-Aware Spatial Regularization and Depth Discontinuity Modeling
PROPOSAL: Incorporate focal-stack-aware spatial regularization and depth discontinuity modeling to improve the robustness and accuracy of DFF-based depth estimation. The approach is inspired by graph-based depth modeling, where edges between neighboring pixels in the image represent depth discontinuities. Design a graph neural network that aggregates features from all focal planes to model long-range depth relationships and incorporates self-supervised learning for distinguishing texture gradients from actual depth changes. This model is trained without ground-truth depth annotations to maintain the unsupervised nature of classical DFF methods. It leverages a knowledge-rich loss formulation that learns to minimize IIPE while correlating inferred edges and depth jumps, all through the preserved spatial smoothness within, as well as overlap and mean squared errors during comparisons across each both-space scale stacks.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Physics-Aware Depth Estimation with Dual-Branch Focus-Attention Network
PROPOSAL: Design a dual-branch focus-attention network that combines spatial and focal information to improve depth estimation from focal stacks. The network will consist of two branches: a conventional convolutional backbone and a novel focus-attention module. The focus-attention module will leverage a physically-inspired focus model to predict the focus-sharpness relationship at each pixel location and scale, and a saliency map to selectively highlight informative focus cues.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed model with state-of-the-art DFF models on the Middlebury and NYU Depth V2 datasets, as well as a baseline model that treats focal-stack images as generic all-in-focus frames.

PREDICTION: The proposed model will improve upon the state-of-the-art DFF models on both datasets, showing robustness in fine-textured and low-texture regions, and reducing noise in depth maps. It may fail to achieve optimal performance when confronted with severely defocused or noisy focal stacks.

TITLE: Robust Transfer Learning with Multi-Task Focal-Stack Training

PREDICTION: The revised approach will improve the robustness of transfer learning by leveraging the joint information in depth and denoising tasks. However, it may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters and may suffer from the increased computational complexity of the multi-task setup.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Depth from Focal-Stacks with Uncertainty-Aware Confidence Ranking
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel approach that estimates the uncertainty of depth predictions from focal stacks using a Bayesian neural network. This will enable the model to provide more robust and reliable depth estimates in challenging scenarios.

PREDICTION: The proposed approach will improve the robustness and reliability of depth estimation by providing uncertainty-aware confidence scores for each pixel. However, it may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters and may suffer from increased computational complexity due to the Bayesian neural network.

TITLE: Comprehensive Cross-Domain Alignment with Multi-Modal Data Fusion

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Learning Focal-Stack Features with Integrated Physics-Informed Supersampling
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a deep learning-based Depth-from-Focus (DFF) method that incorporates physics-informed supersampling to capture the focus-evolution behavior of light in a camera. Specifically, the network takes a focal stack as input and produces a set of refined stacked frames that simulate the defocusing process, from which the depth map is estimated using a combined 3D and 2D convolutional layer. The network is trained on the MPI Sintel Depth Estimation Dataset and the KITTI Depth Estimation Benchmark in end-to-end fashion.
CONTROLS: Comparisons to our baseline model trained on MPI Sintel alone, the state-of-the-art POFD model which also uses depth information, but does not incorporate physics-informed supersampling; compare computational efficiency with the baseline.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We anticipate the proposed physics-informed supersampling model will achieve a gain of ∼0.7% on MPI Sintel and ∼1.2% on the KITTI benchmark over the baseline, with reduced blur and enhanced robustness to unusual focus scenarios. However, we caution that such physics-based methods may implicitly require large-scale optimization resources to capture subtle focus features.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Focal-Stack Inversion via Learned Focal-Statistics Density Estimation
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the use of learned focal-statistics density estimation for focal-stack inversion, allowing the recovery of the focal stack from a single depth map. A density-estimation network is trained on the synthesized multi-focal ImageCLEF Image classification dataset using a hierarchical two-step loss. We hypothesize this allows us to simulate various focal effects in a single model, leading to better performance in real-world depth-estimation applications.
CONTROLS: Compare the learned focal-statistics distribution map (average log sharpness and intensity) against manually crafted statistics; perform ablative analysis with the learned focal-statistics profile.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect to find that learned focal-statistics density estimation significantly improves focal inversion performance, specifically the prediction of blur in edge regions while struggling in flexible-patterned or natural regions.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Focal-Stack Inversion via Learned Focal-Statistics Density Estimation (Revised)
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the use of learned focal-statistics density estimation for focal-stack inversion, allowing the recovery of the focal stack from a single depth map. However, we introduce an additional loss term to handle rare-quality zones encountered in performance-oriented scenarios. Specifically, we introduce an spatial attention mechanism (SAM) and incorporate individually-focal remembered attention adaptability to tackle local supporting network decisions. We retrain our previous model on a modified cross-validation protocol using the ImageCLEF platform.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of SAM with manually-made component affinities; retain ablative analysis with the learned focal-statistics profile, and SMA trials.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We hypothesize improved focal-inversion performance when the rare-quality zones are amortised.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Unsupervised Focal-Stack Analysis using Variational Autoencoders with Physics-Guided Regularization
PROPOSAL: We design a variational autoencoder (VAE) with a physics-guided regularization term that explicitly encourages the latent representation to capture the underlying focal stack characteristics while promoting interpretability and robustness. We explore a novel aspect loss augmented with local attention integrals that captures sharper intermediate effects and aggressively regularizes feature transfer upon retrieval. Comprehensive synthetic and real-world experiments will be used to test the effectiveness of our VAE model.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of our physics-guided loss on interpolability accuracy under down-scale modeled WoW applied on live-scene catastructions on remote-use live-count frames,  assess our methods correlation on used erg-or loaded Hauptbot Finger FurMK uneven Am Ada Hor metadata models for severity measuing Neutral.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect the unsupervised method to demonstrate competitive performance in depth-estimation tasks and extract meaningful latent representations, providing physical insight to plan보다 nearProc-camera initialization sequences. However, this paradigm may fall short due to a lack of fine-grained preferences in rival variants greeting given examples mapped to stubborn local-edge explanations testing rotated stereotypes.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Scene-Aware Multiscale Focal-Stack Modeling with Adaptive Depth Refinement
PROPOSAL: We propose a scene-aware multiscale focal-stack modeling approach that captures the varying focus patterns across different regions of the scene. This is achieved through a novel hierarchical encoder-decoder architecture that adaptively refines the depth estimates at different scales. We integrate a multiscale attention mechanism to selectively focus on regions of high depth uncertainty, leading to more accurate and robust depth maps.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of our multiscale model on indoor and outdoor scenes, using benchmarks such as the NYU-Depth-V2 and Make3D datasets; compare against state-of-the-art focal-stack methods.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect the multiscale model to demonstrate improved depth estimation performance, particularly in scenes with complex depth structures and varying lighting conditions. However, our method may struggle to handle highly textured or transparent regions.

TITLE: Learning to Focus: Investigating a Multitask DFF Model
PROPOSAL: Train a multitask convolutional neural network to jointly predict focal stacks, all-in-focus images, and depth maps from a given input focal stack. The model will have separate branches for each task and will learn to leverage the complementary information contained within the focal stack for improved depth estimation. The multitask loss will be comprised of a combination of mean squared error for depth and a metric learned from a combination of PSNR and SSIM for the all-in-focus images and focal stacks tasks.
CONTROLS: Investigate a baseline model that uses a single task loss for depth estimation and compare the multitask outcome with it, experimentally investigate effect of removal of the focal stacks loss task.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: The multitask model should outperform the baseline model in depth estimation, especially in scenes with complex textures and fine details, but might require a larger amount of training data and a corresponding increase in computational effort.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: "Analyzing Token Distribution in DiTs for Expert Specialization"
PROPOSAL: We will investigate token distribution in visual diffusion transformers to identify potential factors hindering expert specialization. We'll train a Dense DiT on the FFHQ dataset and analyze the distribution of tokens processed by its layers. We'll also compare this distribution to that of a DiT-MoE model, focusing on the frequency and co-occurrence of different tokens, as well as their correlation with network weights and outputs.
CONTROLS: We will compare these results to token distributions in language models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, using their pre-trained weights and a tokenized version of the WikiText-103 dataset as input.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that visual tokens exhibit a more diverse distribution, with less semantic density and stronger spatial dependencies, compared to text tokens, potentially challenging MoE router's ability to learn specialized experts. 

(Juxtaposing results between earlier text model designs with this immediate UX may hinge on theoretical analysis predominating.)

PROPOSAL: We will test whether modifying token choice routing in DiT-MoE can improve expert specialization and quality of generated images. We'll introduce a novel routing scheme that encourages experts to specialize in specific token patterns by integrating a pixel-wise attention mechanism, allowing experts to selectively focus on meaningful regions of the image.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating token-choice routing for Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of two variants of token-choice routing for Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts (DiT-MoE): one where the router selects the top experts at the token level (as in DiT-MoE), and another where it uses a class-agnostic global token-distribution (as in DiffMoE). We will split the input tokens into two groups, where one set of tokens chooses its best experts independently (token-choice), and the other receives the initial predictions of all experts before the router chooses the top ones (skills-all). This allows us to investigate the impact of token-choice routing on expert diversity and activation patterns.
CONTROLS: Two baselines: (1) DiT-MoE with token-choice routing, and (2) a full dense Diffusion Transformer (DiT).
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect the skills-all variant to exhibit more diversity in expert activation patterns and performance, outperforming DiT-MoE in some cases due to better exploration of the network's capacity, but may also lead to quality degradation if the hubs (strongest experts chosen by each token) are over-amplified by late-fusion aggregation.

Please wait for the next turn to revise or add new proposals.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visual Token Classification using Supervised Learning for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: Develop a classification framework to automatically categorize the specialties of patches as they emerge in the diffusion process, to better understand the limitations and opportunities for MoE routing in DiTs. We will fine-tune a pre-trained vision model on a large image dataset to predict the attributes of visual tokens processed by the DiT (e.g., "corner," "texture," "edge," etc.). These attributes will guide expert router training, learning soft-labeled embeddings that capture key features of each expert's learned focus.
CONTROLS: Compare against three ablations: (1) no training, (2) random embeddings, and (3) linear ICA (Independent Component Analysis) for unsupervised classification.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Our approach should cluster tokens into cohesive groups, allowing for more informed routing and thresholding when selecting which experts to process each token, enabling better MoE behavior for tasks like text-to-image generation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Expert Capacity Analysis and Routing Efficiency for MoE Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the capacity of individual experts in MoE Diffusion Transformers and analyze the routing efficiency of the expert router. We will employ a capacity estimation framework, where individual experts are assessed based on their capacity to improve the overall performance of the model. Additionally, we will analyze the routing efficiency of the expert router by evaluating the overlap between the experts' capacities and their actual routing decisions.
CONTROLS: Compare against two expert capacity estimation frameworks: (1) A variant that solely relies on expert weights and (2) a variant that incorporates both expert weights and model gradients.
COST: 10744
PREDICTION: Our analysis will provide insights into the capacity and efficiency of individual experts and provide a comprehensive understanding of expert routing, enabling future research to optimize expert capacity and routing efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating token-choice routing for Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of two variants of token-choice routing for Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts (DiT-MoE): one where the router selects the top experts at the token level (as in DiT-MoE), and another where it uses a class-agnostic global token-distribution (as in DiffMoE). We will split the input tokens into two groups, where one set of tokens chooses its best experts independently (token-choice), and the other receives the initial predictions of all experts before the router chooses the top ones (skills-all). This allows us to investigate the impact of token-choice routing on expert diversity and activation patterns.
CONTROLS: Two baselines: (1) DiT-MoE with token-choice routing, and (2) a full dense Diffusion Transformer (DiT).
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We expect the skills-all variant to exhibit more diversity in expert activation patterns and performance, outperforming DiT-MoE in some cases due to better exploration of the network's capacity, but may also lead to quality degradation if the hubs (strongest experts chosen by each token) are over-amplified by late-fusion aggregation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Token-Level Expert Routing for DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: We modify DiT-MoE to implement token-level routing, where each individual token chooses its top- k experts instead of the batch-level routing. This token-level routing allows us to examine whether different tokens in an image prompt exhibit different behaviors, potentially resulting in more specialized experts.
CONTROLS: We compare this token-level routing DiT-MoE to its original batch-level routing version, as well as a density-matched dense DiT baseline (i.e., a DiT with the same number of active parameters as the MoE version) to verify that MoE leverages model capacity more efficiently.
COST: 12000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that token-level routing can lead to more specialized experts and outperform batch-level routing DiT-MoE. However, it may not reach the level of dense DiT- baselines in high-fidelity tasks due to the increased routing overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mathematical Analysis of Expert Cooperation in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: We prove a lower bound on the regime where expert specialization benefits increase in DiT-MoE, characterized by the trade-off between the diversity of tokens, the similarity of experts' activation patterns, and the quality of the routing mechanism. Specifically, we demonstrate that when tokens follow a certain structural similarity (e.g., contiguous patches in an image), it facilitates more effective expert cooperation, leading to better generation quality.
CONTROLS: Our bound serves as a baseline for future MoE variants that aim to promote expert specialization by taking into account the complex relationships between tokens and experts.
COST: 9000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This mathematical result will provide a foundation for understanding the design principles of MoE for DiTs, and help guide the development of new routing mechanisms that can leverage expert cooperation. However, applying this bound to specific implementation choices remains an open problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Supervised Expert Pre-training for Improved Visual Token Routing
PROPOSAL: We investigate pre-training a set of experts to specialize in visual tokens with distinct characteristics such as texture, color, or edges. During pre-training, a supervisor signals which types of tokens the experts are being tasked with processing. We fine-tune the pre-trained experts in a MoE DiT, where the routing mechanism can leverage the experts' pre-developed specialization.
CONTROLS: We compare the pre-trained experts to randomly initialized experts, as well as those without pre-training. We also evaluate the pre-training benefits in relation to the token-level routing and density-matched dense DiT baselines.
COST: 14000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Pre-training experts to specialize in visual tokens can lead to improved routing and overall generation quality. This approach might mitigate the need for large-scale adaptation of the entire MoE system, nevertheless it could turn out computationally expensive.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Supervised Expert Pre-training for Improved Visual Token Routing
PROPOSAL: We explore variations of the pre-training strategy, including (a) unsupervised pre-training where experts are encouraged to develop intrinsic specialization, (b) multi-task pre-training where multiple tasks (e.g., object detection, segmentation) are fine-tuned simultaneously, and (c) curriculum learning where pre-training difficulty is gradually increased. These adaptations may help alleviate potential over-specialization and promote transfer learning across different tasks.
CONTROLS: We retain the same baselines as before, including token-level routing, batch-level routing, and density-matched dense DiT.
COST: 14641 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Pre-training might add an overhang on MoE routings from over-specialization issues, leading to adverse performance drop, balanced by advancements in MoE reinforcement procedure and thorough tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient MoE Routing via Latent Space Token Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We embed token-level information in a shared latent space and design an MoE router to select experts based on the token embeddings. This allows the router to have a more global understanding of the input token relationships. We further investigate ideas such as using hash functions or fixed-size binning to reduce the dimensionality of the latent space, promoting routing efficiency.
CONTROLS: We compare this method to token-level routing, batch-level routing, and density-matched dense DiT, and analyze whether the latent space embeddings help reduce the routing overhead.
COST: 17000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging the latent space and potentially reducing the dimensionality of token information, the MoE routing of visually dense inputs could become notably more efficient.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Same-Worker, Different-Expert Consistency Regularization
PROPOSAL: We introduce a consistency regularization term to the MoE loss, encouraging the experts to agree on the final output when processing the same token but under different expert properties (e.g., rank, input scale). This regularization promotes consistent behavior within each expert and helps to alleviate the adverse effects of over-specialization.
CONTROLS: We evaluate this approach in conjunction with token-level routing, latent space token embeddings, and compare it to batch-level routing, density-matched dense DiT.
COST: 20000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This regularizer may allow MoE's differences with strong baseline performance to diminish as it encourages cooperation within each worker rather than the overly deep scattering of worker branches away from single problem niches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Token-Routing Heuristics for Expert Specialization in DiTs
PROPOSAL: Examine and evaluate multiple token-routing strategies in Mixture-of-Experts for DiTs, focusing on their ability to facilitate expert specialization and whether they impact performance on generation quality. Specifically, develop routing heuristics based on (1) similarity to cluster centroids, (2) calculated positional dependencies in the token sequence, and (3) learned expert routing indicators that capture relationships between input tokens and experts. Implement and test these heuristics within the EC-DiT framework and report on the achieved expert specialization, with a focus on reduced expert robustness and improved model efficiency. Use the DDPM implementation and train on the 512 × 512 resolution Manga109 dataset.
CONTROLS: Experiment with different hyperparameter settings for embedding dimension, number of experts, and routing indicator selection, as well as baseline EC-DiT performance.
COST: 166.875
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed token-routing strategies to demonstrate improved expert specialization compared to token-choice routing, and that learned routing indicators could lead to more robust model performance.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Measuring and Maximizing Expert Interdependence for MoE in DiTs with Graph-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous proposal to utilize graph-based methods for analyzing expert interdependence in Mixture-of-Experts for Diffusion Transformers. Construct a bipartite graph where experts are nodes and tokens are nodes, with edges representing co-activation and co-firing patterns. Leverage spectral clustering and community detection algorithms to identify groups of interdependent experts and investigate how these clusters relate to task-specific performance. Moreover, use message passing algorithms to implement a symmetric representation learning approach that captures the joint relationships between experts and tokens.
CONTROLS: Evaluate and compare the performance of different graph-based methods and algorithms for capturing expert interdependence and analyze the impact of interdependence on model performance.

PREDICTION: The revised approach using graph-based methods should provide more accurate and robust quantification of expert interdependence, allowing for more effective identification of critical interdependent expert pairs and facilitating better model optimization and adaptation.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Measuring and Maximizing Expert Interdependence for MoE in DiTs with Graph-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous proposal to utilize graph-based methods for analyzing expert interdependence in Mixture-of-Experts for Diffusion Transformers. Construct a bipartite graph where experts are nodes and tokens are nodes, with edges representing co-activation and co-firing patterns. Leverage spectral clustering and community detection algorithms to identify groups of interdependent experts and investigate how these clusters relate to task-specific performance. Moreover, use message passing algorithms to implement a symmetric representation learning approach that captures the joint relationships between experts and tokens.
CONTROLS: Evaluate and compare the performance of different graph-based methods and algorithms for capturing expert interdependence and analyze the impact of interdependence on model performance.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: The revised approach using graph-based methods should provide more accurate and robust quantification of expert interdependence, allowing for more effective identification of critical interdependent expert pairs and facilitating better model optimization and adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Expert Routing for Scalable and Adaptable MoE in DiTs
PROPOSAL: Design a practical expert routing scheme for Mixture-of-Experts in Diffusion Transformers that balances the trade-off between expert specialization and adaptation efficiency. Implement a hierarchical routing mechanism that dynamically selects the expert subset based on the input token distribution, and adaptively updates the routing probabilities using an online estimation approach to capture the evolving interdependence between experts and tokens. Evaluate the proposed routing scheme on real-world datasets and investigate its effectiveness in improving model flexibility and accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline routing schemes and assess the robustness and scalability of the proposed mechanism under varying input distributions and model architectures.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: The practical expert routing scheme should yield significant improvements in model adaptability and accuracy, enabling better specialization of experts and efficient routing decisions under varying input conditions.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: MoE for Sparse DiT Experts: Investigating Hybrid Routing Schemes with Expert Attention Mechanism
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous proposal to incorporate an expert attention mechanism into the hybrid routing scheme for Mixture-of-Experts in Diffusion Transformers. The attention mechanism will learn to focus on the most relevant experts for each input token, further promoting expert specialization and adaptation efficiency. Adapt the existing hybrid routing scheme to incorporate the expert attention mechanism and investigate its impact on model performance and expert interdependence.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effect of the expert attention mechanism on model performance, expert specialization, and interdependence under varying input distributions and model architectures.
COST: 1300
PREDICTION: The addition of the expert attention mechanism should lead to improved expert specialization, reduced over-specialization, and enhanced adaptation efficiency, resulting in better model performance and more robust expert interdependence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying the Expressiveness of MoE in DiTs: A Barrier Error Analysis
PROPOSAL: Develop a barrier error analysis framework to quantify the expressiveness of Mixture-of-Experts in Diffusion Transformers. The framework will decompose the error into multiple components, including the error due to expert misassignment, the error due to expert underutilization, and the error due to intra-expert dissonance. Analyze the expressiveness of MoE in DiTs using this framework and investigate how the proposed expert routing schemes and interdependence measures impact the model's expressiveness.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the framework's performance on a range of tasks and models, and compare the results to a baseline Dense model.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: The barrier error analysis framework should provide valuable insights into the expressiveness of MoE in DiTs, highlighting the need for further improvement in expert routing and interdependence mechanisms to realize the full potential of MoE in diffusion-based models.

ACTION: REVISE 6

TITLE: Investigating Routing Strategies for Expert Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: This experiment will test the impact of different token-routing strategies on expert specialization in a MoE architecture, comparing the effects of simple threshold-based routing, learning-based routing (using a small fully connected network to rank experts), and a more complex learning-based routing (using a transformer autoencoder to learn better expert embeddings).

TITLE: Analyzing the Effects of Token Embedding Design on Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: This experiment evaluates the impact of different token embedding designs on expert specialization, contrasting the effects of fixed embedding spaces, learned embedding adapters, and also a hierarchical token embedding scheme, where tokens are grouped into smaller sets based on learned semantic clusters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline Rehearsal and Episodic Offset Attention
PROPOSAL: We'll extend the rehearsal method from amortised offline meta-learning (ROM) with a new module for estimating the current test-time offset. During rehearsed iterations, we control the environment and incur computational cost to simulate several parallel episodes while adjusting a buffer of past, correspondingly offset observables; during test episodes, we integrate attention mechanisms that weigh the episodic offset history against the standardized training observations in order to adjust on-the-fly our agent's policy, interleaving it with a divergence-generative business-rule-check reinforcement learning module reacting against the persevered pattern-oriented instabilities within the observation function due to past acquisitions. We hypothesise that the interplay between episodic offset attention and ROM would improve robustness in non-stationary environments.
CONTROLS: Imitation learning with batch learning (a common OL-based offline method), state estimation methods (e.g. Kalman and filter basis pursuit denoising) and data augmentation.
COST: 11650
PREDICTION: With standard settings, learning will implicitly encourage our estimator to track past offsets and generalise by employing inductive bias in synthesised episodes instead of resorting to parameter updates tailored to individual environments; our best models won't see if potential knowledge-preserve arrangements substantially impact interoperability at sufficiently-different offsets structures, in particular if space/postings impose an additional discontinuity obstacle despite our topology-friendly approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Collaborative Offset Inference with Hierarchical Attention
PROPOSAL: In complex, multi-dimensional observation spaces with diverse offset patterns, hierarchical attention mechanisms can help our model effectively reason about inter- and intra-dimensional dependencies. By stacking multiple layers of attention modules, we enable the model to selectively focus on subsets of dimensions and/or their sub-components, allowing for more robust and adaptive inference of offset values.
CONTROLS: Differentiable Memory (rev 3), imitation learning without rehearsal, and a state-estimation method with a non-stationary memory model. 
COST: 20560
PREDICTION: Our model should exhibit improved performance in identifying and distinguishing between offset patterns across various dimensions and scales, especially when faced with challenging, multi-modal datasets. However, excessively complex hierarchies might lead to overfitting and decreased generalizability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Episodic Offset Correction with Probabilistic Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: In addition to inferring the prevailing offset pattern, we develop a probabilistic meta-learning framework to estimate the uncertainty associated with each offset prediction. This allows the model to maintain a sense of episodic uncertainty, enabling more informed decision-making in situations where the offset values may be volatile or rapidly changing.
CONTROLS: Collaborative Offset Inference with Hierarchical Attention, Differentiable Memory (rev 3), and imitation learning without rehearsal. 
COST: 26000
PREDICTION: Our approach should lead to improved uncertainty estimation and, by extension, more robust and adaptive decision-making in the face of rapidly changing or uncertain environments. However, the additional computational cost may impact performance in resource-constrained settings, and the probabilistic framework's advantages may be less pronounced in scenarios with well-characterized and stationary offset patterns.

TITLE: Scaling Offline Offset Estimation to Complex Domains with Parallel Learning
PROPOSAL: We introduce a parallel learning framework that decomposes the offset estimation problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems, which can be solved independently across multiple GPUs. This allows us to scale our approach to complex domains, such as robotic manipulation, with hundreds or thousands of degrees of freedom, where efficient parallelization is critical.
CONTROLS: Multi-Agent Fusion for Non-Stationary Offset Estimation, Episodic Offset Correction with Probabilistic Meta-Learning, Collaborative Offset Inference with Hierarchical Attention, Differentiable Memory (rev 3), and Offline Rehearsal and Episodic Offset Attention.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Evaluation of IPC-Nash Q-Learning
PROPOSAL: Implement and evaluate IPC-Nash Q-Learning, a type of offline deep reinforcement learning algorithm, specifically designed to operate in environments with time-varying, per-dimension additive offsets. IPC-Nash learns to balance the exploitation of expected long-term rewards with exploration for update priorities. We will evaluate its performance on a selection of robot navigation and manipulation tasks in a synthetic environment where the observation function evolves according to a piecewise linear function.
CONTROLS: Compare with dueling Double Q-Learning and IPC-Reward with maximum exploration rate.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: IPC-Nash Q-learning will report competitive performance, balancing exploration and exploitation under noisy or shifted observations, and withstanding shifts in the observation function not seen during offline RL training. It might struggle when the noise distribution is far from Gaussian or the shifts exhibit complex patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Non-Parametric State Estimation with Learned Offsets
PROPOSAL: Develop a non-parametric state estimation method that uses IPC-Nash Q-learning to learn the offsets from data and update them online in a stream of new observations. We will leverage a nearest neighbors distance-based algorithm, such as K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), along with a changing kernel, based on increase in error in successive estimations. This new method will be trained and tested on a range of realistic, synthetic environments with time-varying offsets.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed non-parametric method against parametric estimators for standard and extreme noise patterns.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Perform better under significant noise and offsets that have complex, abrupt, non-Gaussian patterns than parametric state estimators which rely heavily on assumptions about the distribution. But KNN-based method will not align data points under wounded external formulation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline Robust Eigendynamics Learning for Episodic Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: 
We propose using Offline Robust Eigendynamics Learning (O-REL), a technique that trains a policy on a stationary offline dataset to learn the eigendynamics of the observation function, as they govern the directions in which the offsets' effects are mainly summarized. By leveraging spectral properties, O-REL is robust against abrupt, non-Markovian shifts in the observation function, providing a compact representation that captures how per-dimension offsets influence the agent's perception of the environment. O-REL consists of a pre-training stage where an offline RL model learns a basic representation from the stationary dataset, followed by a spectral analysis to determine the observation function's fundamental properties. It then fine-tunes the model by incorporating an offset compensation correction signal into the policy learning process. We show how O-REL effectively captures the eigendynamics of arbitrarily complex real-world time-series patterns of non-stationarity within the observation function, ensuring the learned policy acts robustly even when each episode begins with unnormalized observation functions, exhibiting unknown shifts.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline Offline RL models trained without capturing episodic non-stationarity, such as Q-learning and SARSA
- A-REL, the MARL-inspired variant without spectral analysis that instead relies on a preculculated offset estimation
- Online-adaptation via RL as a baseline to address unseen non-stationarity for costly environments
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: 
Offline-RL convergence using O-REL, with robust performance in both stationary and non-stationary environments scoring 1.2x improvement in both metrics considered – action success rate (ASR) and task completion metrics – over standard offline RL models when unseen episodes of non-stationarity are introduced; however novelty or unpredictability in the patterns could limit its effectiveness.

PROPOSAL: 
We introduce Hyper-Spectral Model Distillation (HSMD), a novel approach to efficiently leverage spectral analysis in offline non-stationary robust RL by distilling knowledge from a large pre-trained offline RL model into a more compact form. This enables fast and effective adaptation to unknown shifts in the observation function, reducing the need for computationally expensive retraining. HSMD retains the essential eigenvectors of the learned policy while prescribing a new weighting strategy that captures the strength of each eigenvector, allowing for the construction of a smaller, more efficient distilled model. We train HSMD on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

TITLE: CLip: Causal Latent Shift Inference for Offline Non-Stationary Adversarial Environments
PROPOSAL: 
We revise CLip to incorporate a staged regularization scheme that reduces overfitting in the presence of complex time-series patterns of non-stationarity. The revised CLip now uses an adaptive iterative incorporation process that manages interpretability pruning from novel progressive adaptation phases, adjusting the strength of regularization progressively as learning gathers more local master knowledge environment inducing recommendations. This enhancement enables CLip to better address challenges in real-world applications, such as robotics and healthcare, where complex and unpredictable non-stationarity patterns are common. We train and evaluate the revised CLip on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its improved performance in handling complex non-stationarity patterns.
CONTROLS: 
- Original CLip model without regularization
- CLip models with different regularization strengths
- Online-adaptation via RL as a baseline to address complex unseen non-stationarity for costly environments
COST: 2880
PREDICTION: 
The revised CLip model will exhibit improved robustness and adaptability in the presence of complex non-stationarity patterns, outperforming the original CLip model and baseline methods in both synthetic and real-world experiments. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with extremely complex or adversarial patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reinforcement Learning with Temporal Shift Invariant Neural Networks (TSINNs)
PROPOSAL: 
We propose the use of Temporal Shift Invariant Neural Networks (TSINNs) in reinforcement learning to address non-stationarity in the observation function. TSINNs are designed to learn representations that are invariant to temporal shifts, allowing them to capture the underlying dynamics of the environment while ignoring the noisy and non-stationary offset. By training a TSINN-based policy on a stationary offline dataset, theagent can develop a robust and generalizable representation of the environment that is immune to the effects of non-stationarity at test time. We experiment with TSINNs on various robot navigation tasks and compare their performance to state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning methods.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline REINFORCE model without TSINN
- TSINNs with and without offset correction
- Offline RL models that assume perfect knowledge of the offset
COST: 3680
PREDICTION: 
The TSINN-based policy will exhibit improved robustness and generalizability in the presence of non-stationarity, outperforming baseline REINFORCE models and showing competitive results with offline RL methods that assume perfect knowledge of the offset. However, the performance of TSINNs may degrade in scenarios with extremely complex or adversarial non-stationarity patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distilling Episodic Robustness in Offline Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a technique for distilling the episodic robustness of offline reinforcement learning policies, allowing the agent to retain its robustness to non-stationarity across multiple episodes without the need for extensive fine-tuning. The proposed method leverages a pre-trained offline RL model and employs an episodic robustness distillation process to mimic the behavior of the robust policy on a set of carefully crafted robustness metrics. The distilled policy can then be used as a starting point for additional training, eliminating the need for extensive fine-tuning on each new episode. We evaluate the proposed method on various offline RL benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in retaining episodic robustness while improving sample efficiency.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline offline RL models without distillation
- Offline RL models with and without fine-tuning
- Online-adaptation via RL as a baseline to address unseen non-stationarity for costly environments
COST: 5280
PREDICTION: 
The distilled policy will exhibit improved robustness and sample efficiency, outperforming baseline offline RL models and reducing the need for extensive fine-tuning on each new episode. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with extremely complex or adversarial non-stationarity patterns requiring significant fine-tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Task Adaptation for Offline Reinforcement Learning with Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a meta-learning approach to adapt to new tasks and non-stationarity patterns in offline reinforcement learning. Our method, Meta-TASK-Ada, uses a meta-objective function to optimize the policy's performance across a range of tasks and non-stationarity patterns, allowing it to adapt to new unseen cases at test time. We introduce a task-space learning strategy that updates the policy's parameters based on the difference between the expected and observed performance of the policy on each new task. This allows the policy to adapt to new tasks and non-stationarity patterns without the need for extensive fine-tuning. We evaluate Meta-TASK-Ada on various offline RL benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in adapting to new tasks and non-stationarity patterns.

- Offline RL models with and without task-space learning

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning with Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a transfer learning approach for offline reinforcement learning with non-stationarity. Our method, Trans-learn, leverages the idea of transferring knowledge from a source task to a target task with non-stationarity. We introduce a two-stage framework: (1) self-supervised learning of transferable representations from a large corpus of data, and (2) target-task adaptation using the learned transferable representations. We evaluate Trans-learn on various offline RL benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in transferring knowledge across tasks with non-stationarity.

- Offline RL models with and without self-supervised learning
- Online-adaptation via RL as a baseline to address unseen non-stationarity for costly environments

TITLE: Reinforcement Learning with Temporal Shift Invariant Neural Networks (TSINNs)
PROPOSAL: 
We propose the use of Temporal Shift Invariant Neural Networks (TSINNs) in reinforcement learning to address non-stationarity in the observation function. TSINNs are designed to learn representations that are invariant to temporal shifts, allowing them to capture the underlying dynamics of the environment while ignoring the noisy and non-stationary offset. By training a TSINN-based policy on a stationary offline dataset, theagent can develop a robust and generalizable representation of the environment that is immune to the effects of non-stationarity at test time. We experiment with TSINNs on various robot navigation tasks and compare their performance to state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Distilling Episodic Robustness in Offline Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a technique for distilling the episodic robustness of offline reinforcement learning policies, allowing the agent to retain its robustness to non-stationarity across multiple episodes without the need for extensive fine-tuning. The proposed method leverages a pre-trained offline RL model and employs an episodic robustness distillation process to mimic the behavior of the robust policy on a set of carefully crafted robustness metrics. The distilled policy can then be used as a starting point for additional training, eliminating the need for extensive fine-tuning on each new episode. We evaluate the proposed method on various offline RL benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in retaining episodic robustness while improving sample efficiency.

- Online-adaptation via RL as a baseline to address unseen non-stationarity for costly environments

TITLE: Meta-Task Adaptation for Offline Reinforcement Learning with Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a meta-learning approach to adapt to new tasks and non-stationarity patterns in offline reinforcement learning. Our method, Meta-TASK-Ada, uses a meta-objective function to optimize the policy's performance across a range of tasks and non-stationarity patterns, allowing it to adapt to new unseen cases at test time. We introduce a task-space learning strategy that updates the policy's parameters based on the difference between the expected and observed performance of the policy on each new task. This allows the policy to adapt to new tasks and non-stationarity patterns without the need for extensive fine-tuning. We evaluate Meta-TASK-Ada on various offline RL benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in adapting to new tasks and non-stationarity patterns.

- Baseline offline RL models without meta-learning
- Online-adaptation via RL as a baseline to address unseen non-stationarity for costly environments
- Offline RL models with and without task-space learning

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning with Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a transfer learning approach for offline reinforcement learning with non-stationarity. Our method, Trans-learn, leverages the idea of transferring knowledge from a source task to a target task with non-stationarity. We introduce a two-stage framework: (1) self-supervised learning of transferable representations from a large corpus of data, and (2) target-task adaptation using the learned transferable representations. We evaluate Trans-learn on various offline RL benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in transferring knowledge across tasks with non-stationarity.

PROPOSAL: Train agents on stationary offline data augmented with a self-supervised stratification of observations into episodes, where each episode corresponds to a set of state-action pairs with temporally correlated observations. Evaluate agents on real-world, synthetic, and simulated environments with normally distributed, realistic offsets. Analyze performance on a low-dimensional robot navigation task (Virtual PR2 simulations) and a high-dimensional robot manipulation task (Real-World Franka Emika Panda Robot).

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Offset-Invariant Priors for Offline RL: Meta-Learning to Forget Partly Observed Temporal Patterns
PROPOSAL: Train offline agents to learn Offset-Invariant Priors (OIPs) that embed observation functions under various partially observed temporal patterns, factored out from temporally invariant ones, allowing for adaptation to unseen non-stationarity at test time. OIPs are learned via normalizing flows on the embedded observations and are shared across episodes and conditions. Evaluate agents on synthetic and real-world environments with multiple episodes and unknown time-series patterns of non-stationarity.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Embed-to-Prediction via Temporal Observation Representations for Offline RL in Non-Stationary Environments
PROPOSAL: Introduce Temporal Observation Representations (TORs) that map sequences of observations into fixed-length embeddings, capturing temporal patterns within and across episodes, for offline RL. TORs bridge the gap between the non-stationary observation space and the stationary offline RL setup, allowing agents to learn robust policies using observations from multiple episodes. Evaluate TORs on robotic manipulation tasks (synthetic Franka Emika Panda Robot) and robot navigation tasks (synthetic PR2).
CONTROLS: Compare to Baseline 1, Baseline 2, Proposal 1, and Proposal 2 (Offset-Invariant Priors for Offline RL: Meta-Learning to Forget Partly Observed Temporal Patterns).

PREDICTION: Expected results: 8-10% improvement over the baselines, 2-4% improvement over Proposal 1, and comparable performance with Proposal 2, particularly on manipulation tasks, where TORs can better capture variations in object state and robot observations, failing to generalize to environments with extremely variable or high-dimensional observation spaces.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Embed-to-Prediction via Temporal Observation Representations for Offline RL in Non-Stationary Environments with Offset-Informed Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Introduce Offset-Informed Embeddings (OIEs) to the TORs of Proposal 3 by incorporating per-episode offset information as a contextual marker for the embedding process, allowing TORs to better account for offset-induced temporal discrepancies in the observation space. Evaluate OIE-TORs on robotic manipulation tasks (synthetic Franka Emika Panda Robot) and robot navigation tasks (synthetic PR2), including episodes with varying offset distributions and sequence lengths.
CONTROLS: Compare to Baseline 1, Baseline 2, Proposal 1, Proposal 2, and Revised Proposal 3 (Embed-to-Prediction via Temporal Observation Representations for Offline RL in Non-Stationary Environments without OIEs).
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: Expected results: 4-6% improvement over the baselines and 1-2% improvement over Revised Proposal 3, particularly on tasks with dynamic or unknown offsets, where OIEs can adjust the embedding process to reflect changes in the observation space, failing to generalize to neglected offset variances or inconsistent estimation of OIEs.

ACTION: ADD 4

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Novel Dataset for Offline Non-Stationary RL with Time-Varying Offsets
PROPOSAL: Generate a new dataset, "Offset Nav" and "Offset Manip", which will focus on robot navigation and robot manipulation respectively. Each dataset will consist of numerous episodes, where the observation function is shifted by time-varying, per-dimension additive offsets following complex real-world time-series patterns. Training and test episodes will be generated using different sets of offsets.
CONTROLS: Provide a stationary environment dataset (e.g. "Gym Navigation-v0") as a baseline for comparison.
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: This dataset will provide a challenging test environment for offline RL methods to handle non-stationarity within the observation function. The performance of methods on this dataset could fail when encountering offsets that are highly non-linear or sparse in time.

PROPOSAL: Adopt meta-Reinforcement learning (meta-RL) to train a model on various scenarios, where each scenario represents a different offset pattern. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Token By-Elimination for Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Investigate a token-by-elimination mechanism that actively removes tokens from the sequence for text-based reasoning steps, while continuing to generate and consume visual tokens. Specifically, we will modify the generation process to opportunistically delete surplus text tokens after each reasoning step, aggregating their content into a more efficient representation. This approach can potentially reduce chain lengths, alleviate training and inference costs, and promote coherence in the generated images. We will evaluate this approach on a range of tasks, including reasoning-driven text-to-image generation and instruction-based image editing.
CONTROLS: Baseline is a standard sequence-to-sequence model without any token-by-elimination mechanism.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: This approach should lead to improved training efficiency and inference speed, particularly on longer reasoning chains. However, it may also induce additional risk of token omission, conflicting with the need for accurate reasoning flows.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Efficient Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Graph-Based Sequence Modeling
PROPOSAL:  Design and evaluate a novel CoT-LLMs (Large-Language-Models) architecture, referred to as CoT-Graph, that leverages a graph attention mechanism to process the interdependencies between textual reasoning steps and visual state transitions. CoT-Graph operates by 1) computing graph representations for both text and visual inputs, 2) applying graph attention to identify interdependencies, and 3) incorporating the graph embedding into the sequence-to-sequence CoT framework. The experiment assesses CoT-Graph's performance on the landscape image generation from topographic contour maps and instruction-based image editing tasks.
CONTROLS:  Investigate the impact of entity and relationship attention in the graph attention layer, as well as slice-based sampling of intermediate graphs during generation to avoid the quadratic scaling of standard graph neural networks.
COST: 15050
PREDICTION:  The proposed CoT-Graph architecture should demonstrate improved model efficiency and abductive reasoning capabilities, complemented by effective visual and text-based inference, thus achieving state-of-the-art results on the selected tasks with significantly reduced computational costs.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Vision and Language (CoTVL) Benchmark
PROPOSAL: Establish a new benchmark, CoTVL-Benchmark, which combines several existing real-world datasets for reasoning-driven tasks (e.g., Visual Question Answering, Jigsaw Puzzle Solving, Landscape Image Generation from Topographic Contour Maps) and proposes challenging new tasks (e.g., instruction-based image editing). CoTVL-Benchmark assesses models using both classification accuracy and auxiliary metrics (e.g., fluency of intermediate steps, similarity between steps and the final result).
CONTROLS: Our baseline control model is BERT-large, fine-tuned on the overlapping text and visual components of the CoTVL-Benchmark datasets. Additional ablations will be run on variants of our proposed CoTVL model architecture (to be introduced in Turn 2) with and without certain features like ground-truth-based masking or instance-specific adaptations.
COST: 120,000
PREDICTION: Experiments on CoTVL-Benchmark are expected to reveal weaknesses in leading MLLMs and demonstrate the significance of our research direction. The greatest risk lies in performing poorly on unseen tasks where our baseline might seem reasonably competent (e.g., topographic map generation from text descriptions), hampering the perceived value of the proposed CoTVL framework for large-scale vision-language pre-training.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Unified Chain-of-Thought Transformers for Unified Textual-Visual Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Present the CoTVL Transformer, a novel model architecture that jointly reinforces text generation, vision generation, and reasoning. CoTVL Trainer trains the model directly with a proposed cross-modal loss, minimizing a mixture of textual loss, visual loss, and an auxiliary reasoning loss measuring similarity between intermediates and the final answer. The reasoning loss helps guide the model to create coherent step-by-step reasoning flows.
CONTROLS: The baseline control model will be the Masked Language Model (MLM) re-purposed for our CoTVL-Benchmark tasks, exploiting modifications and fine-tuning to infill missing terms and objects within unseen images. Additionally, ablations will be conducted to investigate the necessity of the auxiliary reasoning loss and visual encoder fine-tuning.
COST: 434,000
PREDICTION: Our hypothesis is that the CoTVL Transformer outperforms both vanilla MLLMs and reasoning-ignore baselines by a significant margin in CoTVL-Benchmark. We might, however, confront difficulties with reproducing and validating performance on rare cases where visual pattern-matching plays a very crucial role (e.g., applying abstract transformations).

PROPOSAL: To further enhance the performance of our Unified Chain-of-Thought Transformers, we introduce an alternative to the pipeline Ring-Refining Mechanism. This revised mechanism uses a Content-Agnostic Variational Encoding (CAVE) approach, which integrates uncertainty estimation and spatial reasoning to guide the refinement process. By leveraging CAVE, our model can:
1. Enhance the generation of coherent intermediate steps that accurately describe the visual reasoning process.
2. Improve the overall performance and stability of the model, especially in scenarios with long, compositional reasoning chains.

This is achieved by refining the model's ability to integrate information from both textual and visual modalities, leading to improved visual state transition reasoning.

TITLE: Visio-Linguistic Reasoning with Visually-Grounded Attention
PROPOSAL: To improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the Unified Chain-of-Thought Transformers, we propose a Visio-Linguistic Reasoning (VLR) module that grounds attention in visual information. VLR targets weak points in the inference process by incorporating visually-grounded attention, which enhances the modal fusion and facilitates the learning of relevant object-perceptual structures.

In VLR, attention weights are computed as a product of visual and linguistic features. This visually-grounded attention allows the model to:

2. Reduce the reliance on language-only attention, which can lead to incomplete or incorrect reasoning.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Knowledge Integration and Abstraction in Visio-Linguistic Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the Visio-Linguistic Reasoning (VLR) module, we propose a novel knowledge integration and abstraction framework. This framework enables the model to efficiently integrate and abstract high-level visual and linguistic knowledge to support visual reasoning tasks. The framework consists of:

1. Visual Abstraction Network (VAN): A neural network that abstracts high-level visual features from the input image.
2. Linguistic Abstraction Network (LAN): A neural network that abstracts high-level linguistic features from the input text.
3. Knowledge Fusion Module (KFM): A module that integrates the abstracted visual and linguistic features to form a compact knowledge representation.

The knowledge representation is then used to guide the visual reasoning process and improve the performance of the VLR module.

CONTROLS: To evaluate the effectiveness of the knowledge integration and abstraction framework, we conduct comprehensive experiments on tasks from the CoTVL-Benchmark, including visual question answering, visual reasoning, and image generation. We also compare the performance of the VLR module with and without the framework.

PREDICTION: The knowledge integration and abstraction framework is expected to significantly improve the performance of the Visio-Linguistic Reasoning module on visual reasoning tasks. However, we may face challenges in tuning the framework's parameters to achieve optimal results on specific tasks.

TITLE: Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Vision and Language (CoTVL) Benchmark
PROPOSAL: Establish a new benchmark, CoTVL-Benchmark, which combines several existing real-world datasets for reasoning-driven tasks (e.g., Visual Question Answering, Jigsaw Puzzle Solving, Landscape Image Generation from Topographic Contour Maps) and proposes challenging new tasks (e.g., instruction-based image editing). CoTVL-Benchmark assesses models using both classification accuracy and auxiliary metrics (e.g., fluency of intermediate steps, similarity between steps and the final result).
CONTROLS: Our baseline control model is BERT-large, fine-tuned on the overlapping text and visual components of the CoTVL-Benchmark datasets. Additional ablations will be run on variants of our proposed CoTVL model architecture (to be introduced in Turn 2) with and without certain features like ground-truth-based masking or instance-specific adaptations.
COST: 360,000
PREDICTION: Experiments on CoTVL-Benchmark are expected to reveal weaknesses in leading MLLMs and demonstrate the significance of our research direction. The greatest risk lies in performing poorly on unseen tasks where our baseline might seem reasonably competent (e.g., topographic map generation from text descriptions), hampering the perceived value of the proposed CoTVL framework for large-scale vision-language pre-training.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Unified CoT with Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Train a T0-like large language model to generate a sequence of textual intermediates and associated visual outputs on tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and instruction-based image editing. PREDICTION: Large improvements in multi-task performance due to shared and more cohesive image-generation patterns, boosted performance on reasoning tasks, and internal evaluation pointing to better image-wise understanding and generation quality. However, differences may be harder to observe in 'solo' tasks and special mission scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Egocentric MLLMs' Ability to Understand User Intent with Gaze Cues
PROPOSAL:  Compare state-of-the-art egocentric video question answering models (e.g. VisDial-G, Gqa-XL) on epistemic exams (difficulty level can indicate truly challenging questions), but evaluate them exclusively on a dataset with both exocentric and egocentric video modalities paired with associated human gaze data (Adding sample annotations from publicly available egocentric datasets (e.g. Egocentric Pedestrian Detection, DIPETE Dataset))
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: only exocentric video, Baseline 2: only human gaze as input
COST: 400
PREDICTION: MLLMs without access to user gaze information will show significant performance drops on egocentric video question answering exams, as the presence of gaze cues can increase accuracy on difficult questions, which are where egocentric MLLMs are generally weak. 

They will begin noticing these performance drops on the hard questions that mostly belong to egocentric perspective and resultantly show that reliable understanding of user intent through egocentric perspective requires the integration of visual perception and gaze cues.

TITLE: Assessing Egocentric Gaze for Personalized Proactive AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: Evaluate a state-of-the-art egocentric video question answering model (e.g. VisDial-G, Gqa-XL) on a proactive dialog dataset (e.g. Proactive Egocentric Dialog Dataset) paired with human ground-truth user intent, explicitly incorporating both user gaze information and a pre-trained gaze estimation model for accurate gaze detection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Signal Accuracy on Egocentric MLLM Performance
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of an egocentric video question answering model trained on both user gaze information and a gaze estimation model, on another model trained with noisy gaze data (simulating imperfect gaze tracking), on another model with well-estimated but mislabeled gaze signals (e.g. same eye-tracking location for every seen region of interest). We will utilize a dataset with both accurate and noisy gaze data from egocentric video.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: no gaze information, Baseline 2: per-utterance true gaze changes and well-estimated gaze initiation
COST: 560
PREDICTION: The results of this experiment will show the sensitivity of MLLMs to the accuracy of gaze data when it comes to answering questions from an egocentric user perspective. If the errors in gaze tracking data are high, then the model trained with these noisy data may perform similarly to the baseline model with no gaze data at all. We expect the reduction in performance as the quality of the gaze signal is degraded.

CONTROLS: Baseline 1: only exocentric video, Baseline 2: only human gaze as input

PREDICTION: MLLMs without access to user gaze information will show significant performance drops on egocentric video question answering exams, as the presence of gaze cues can increase accuracy on difficult questions, which are where egocentric MLLMs are generally weak. 

They will begin noticing these performance drops on the hard questions that mostly belong to egocentric perspective and resultantly show that reliable understanding of user intent through egocentric perspective requires the integration of visual perception and gaze cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Egocentric Gaze for Personalized Proactive AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: Evaluate a state-of-the-art egocentric video question answering model (e.g. VisDial-G, Gqa-XL) on a proactive dialog dataset (e.g. Proactive Egocentric Dialog Dataset) paired with human ground-truth user intent, explicitly incorporating both user gaze information and a pre-trained gaze estimation model for accurate gaze detection. 
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: only user input and model output, Baseline 2: only egocentric video input
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating user gaze information will improve proactive dialog flow for AI assistants, as the user's focus and intent can be more accurately captured and predicted, leading to more seamless and proactive user experience. This result will provide crucial evidence that MLLMs can be used to create AI assistants that better understand user intent and require less user input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Signal Accuracy on Egocentric MLLM Performance
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of an egocentric video question answering model trained on both user gaze information and a gaze estimation model, on another model trained with noisy gaze data (simulating imperfect gaze tracking), on another model with well-estimated but mislabeled gaze signals (e.g. same eye-tracking location for every seen region of interest). We will utilize a dataset with both accurate and noisy gaze data from egocentric video.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: no gaze information, Baseline 2: per-utterance true gaze changes and well-estimated gaze initiation
COST: 1700
PREDICTION: The results of this experiment will show the sensitivity of MLLMs to the accuracy of gaze data when it comes to answering questions from an egocentric user perspective. If the errors in gaze tracking data are high, then the model trained with these noisy data may perform similarly to the baseline model with no gaze data at all. We expect the reduction in performance as the quality of the gaze signal is degraded.

We will also include ablations of the model's visual processing component and memory component to understand which part of the model is most affected by the lack of gaze information. COST: 120000
PREDICTION: We expect the model's performance to degrade significantly on the egocentric video task without gaze information, especially on tasks that require understanding user intent. However, the model may still perform well on tasks that primarily require scene understanding. This could fail if the egocentric video dataset without gaze information has a very different distribution from the standard egocentric video question answering task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Egocentric Video Question Answering with Gaze Cues
PROPOSAL: Design and release a new egocentric video question answering benchmark, EGOCRAFT, which includes explicit gaze cues and requires models to infer user intentions from the combination of visual and gaze information. We will use the EGOCRAFT benchmark to evaluate the performance of existing large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on understanding user intent, comparing them to the performance on the popular EgovidQ benchmark without gaze information. Additionally, we will fine-tune a selection of MLLMs on the EGOCRAFT benchmark to see if the inclusion of gaze information improves performance on tasks requiring user intention inference.
CONTROLS: We will baseline the performance of popular MLLMs (e.g., BlenderBot3, OPT, and LLaMA) on both EGOCRAFT and EgovidQ benchmarks without gaze information. Ablation studies will be performed to evaluate the impact of gaze information on user intention inference tasks. Compare the performance of LLMs without explicit gaze modeling against MLLMs, and study the trade-off between performance and computational cost when using gaze-related information.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: We expect existing MLLMs to perform poorly on EGOCRAFT, despite their strong performance on EgovidQ, highlighting the importance of gaze information in detecting user intentions from egocentric views. Fine-tuning on EGOCRAFT is expected to lead to significant improvements in user intention inference tasks when gaze information is explicitly included, showcasing the potential benefits of gaze-aided user intent understanding.

This study will help us understand the most effective way to incorporate gaze information into MLLMs.

This study will help us understand how to mitigate the influence of poor gaze signal accuracy on MLLMs.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Quantifying Inter-Modal Gradients with Layer-Wise Energy Distance
PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel layer-wise energy distance (LWED) metric to quantify the disagreement between text and vision gradients within a modality-shared AR transformer. LWED measures the difference in probability distributions between feature activations of the text and vision tokens at different transformer layers. We will demonstrate LWED's effectiveness by computing its values for two pre-trained AR UMMs (DALL-E and BlenderBot) on a range of benchmark tasks, including image captioning and segmentation.
CONTROLS: We will compare LWED's performance to that of a variety of standard evaluation metrics (e.g., BLEU, cosine similarity, and mutual information) on the same tasks and datasets.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: LWED should reveal significant layer-wise differences in inter-modal gradients, highlighting regions of conflict and identifying opportunities for modality-aware optimization. It may struggle to capture nuanced, high-level semantics due to its focus on feature activations.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating Gradient Conflicts in AR UMMs with Synthetic Evaluation Datasets
PROPOSAL: We will create a set of carefully engineered synthetic evaluation datasets (SEDs) to systematically study the effects of gradient conflicts on AR UMMs. SEDs will include controlled examples of modality-conflict scenarios, such as heavily occluded or conceptually mismatched images, where we can precisely vary the degree of conflict between text and vision tokens. Our main goal is to analyze how different training objectives, optimization algorithms, and transformer configurations respond to these conflicts, identifying the most critical factors influencing model performance and trainability.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of standard AR UMMs (e.g., DALL-E) and a modified version equipped with a modality-aware gradient averaging technique, which we expect will mitigate gradient conflicts.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: By analyzing SEDs, we should be able to pinpoint the main sources of gradient conflicts and ineffective model behavior, guiding the development of more robust and efficient AR UMMs. However, over-engineering of the SEDs might lead to misleading results or inaccurate generalization to real-world data.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Factorized Autoencoding for Modality-Invariant Representations
PROPOSAL: We propose Factorized Autoencoding (FA), a novel approach to extract modality-invariant representations from modality-shared AR transformers. FA learns separate, yet aligned, encoding spaces for text and vision tokens through a factorized process that alternates between autoregressive reconstruction and modality-invariant regularization. Our goal is to create a hidden representation space that reduces gradient conflicts by minimizing the divergence between modality-specific encoding distributions.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of FA to standard AR UMMs, as well as a modality-aware variant that employs a modality-specific bottleneck.
COST: 5600
PREDICTION: By leveraging factorized autoencoding, we expect to significantly reduce gradient conflicts and improve the quality of representations in modality-shared AR transformers. However, FA might experience representational compromise due to the restrictive bottleneck imposed by modality-invariant regularization.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised SEDs and a Configurable Multi-Task Training Framework
PROPOSAL: We refine our previously proposed synthetic evaluation datasets (SEDs) and introduce a modular, configurable multi-task training framework to systematically analyze the effects of gradient conflicts on AR UMMs. Our revised SEDs incorporate a wide range of real-world datasets, such as ImageNet and COCO, and include specific task-focused scenarios (e.g., text-to-image generation and visual question answering). The modular framework enables effortless extension and modification of training objectives, optimization algorithms, and transformer configurations, facilitating in-depth studies of the complex interplay between gradient conflicts and task performance.
CONTROLS: We continue to compare the performance of standard AR UMMs against a modality-aware gradient averaging technique and will investigate the impact of our revised SEDs on model behavior.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: The revised SEDs and modular framework should provide rich insights into the performance of AR UMMs under diverse real-world scenarios, leading to more robust training configurations and mitigating gradient conflicts. However, the complexity of the framework may come at the cost of additional computational requirements and training time.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Intermediate Layers in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of ablation studies to investigate the role of intermediate layers in modality-shared AR transformers. By selectively removing or disabling different layers from the transformer architecture, we can quantify the impact of intermediate layer representation uncertainty on gradient conflicts and task performance. Our main goal is to understand whether and how intermediate layers contribute to modality conflicts and to develop strategies for optimizing and adapting these layers to specific tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of varying layer configurations to that of a standard AR UMM, focusing on tasks that are sensitive to intermediate layer representations, such as visual question answering.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: By analyzing the effects of intermediate layer configuration on gradient conflicts and task performance, we expect to gain valuable insights into the role of these layers in modality-shared AR transformers. However, the importance of these layers may vary depending on the task and dataset, making the implications of our findings not universally applicable.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Modality Conflict Reduction
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial training method to mitigate modality conflicts in AR UMMs. By introducing an adversary that attempts to manipulate the input modalities to lead to conflicting gradients, we can encourage the AR UMM to adapt and learn more modality-invariant representations. Our main goal is to assess the effectiveness of adversarial training in reducing modality conflicts and improving performance on a range of tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of adversarial training to that of standard AR UMMs and other state-of-the-art methods that address modality conflicts, such as factorized autoencoding.
COST: 8300
PREDICTION: Adversarial training may help reduce modality conflicts by encouraging the AR UMM to learn more robust and invariant representations. However, the potential for overfitting to the adversary's manipulation strategy and the time-consuming nature of adversarial training pose challenges to its practical application.
