TITLE: Multi-modal Knowledge Distillation for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-modal knowledge distillation framework to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained AR UMM to a smaller AR UMM. Our framework combines knowledge distillation and teacher-student learning to transfer knowledge across modalities, with a focus on minimizing modality conflict. We will evaluate the effectiveness of our framework on several AR UMM tasks, including text-to-image generation and visual question answering.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of multi-modal knowledge distillation to other knowledge distillation methods and teacher-student learning methods.
COST: 12656
PREDICTION: Our multi-modal knowledge distillation framework should improve the performance of AR UMMs on various tasks, while reducing modality conflict. However, the effectiveness of knowledge distillation may depend on the quality of the pre-trained teacher model, and additional efforts may be required to adapt the framework to specific AR UMM tasks.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Quantifying Inter-Modal Gradients with Layer-Wise Energy Distance
PROPOSAL: We will propose a novel layer-wise energy distance (LWED) metric to quantify the disagreement between text and vision gradients within a modality-shared AR transformer. LWED measures the difference in probability distributions between feature activations of the text and vision tokens at different transformer layers. We will demonstrate LWED's effectiveness by computing its values for two pre-trained AR UMMs (DALL-E and BlenderBot) on a range of benchmark tasks, including image captioning and segmentation.
CONTROLS: We will compare LWED's performance to that of a variety of standard evaluation metrics (e.g., BLEU, cosine similarity, and mutual information) on the same tasks and datasets.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: LWED should reveal significant layer-wise differences in inter-modal gradients, highlighting regions of conflict and identifying opportunities for modality-aware optimization. It may struggle to capture nuanced, high-level semantics due to its focus on feature activations.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating Gradient Conflicts in AR UMMs with Synthetic Evaluation Datasets
PROPOSAL: We will create a set of carefully engineered synthetic evaluation datasets (SEDs) to systematically study the effects of gradient conflicts on AR UMMs. SEDs will include controlled examples of modality-conflict scenarios, such as heavily occluded or conceptually mismatched images, where we can precisely vary the degree of conflict between text and vision tokens. Our main goal is to analyze how different training objectives, optimization algorithms, and transformer configurations respond to these conflicts, identifying the most critical factors influencing model performance and trainability.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of standard AR UMMs (e.g., DALL-E) and a modified version equipped with a modality-aware gradient averaging technique, which we expect will mitigate gradient conflicts.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: By analyzing SEDs, we should be able to pinpoint the main sources of gradient conflicts and ineffective model behavior, guiding the development of more robust and efficient AR UMMs. However, over-engineering of the SEDs might lead to misleading results or inaccurate generalization to real-world data.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Factorized Autoencoding for Modality-Invariant Representations
PROPOSAL: We propose Factorized Autoencoding (FA), a novel approach to extract modality-invariant representations from modality-shared AR transformers. FA learns separate, yet aligned, encoding spaces for text and vision tokens through a factorized process that alternates between autoregressive reconstruction and modality-invariant regularization. Our goal is to create a hidden representation space that reduces gradient conflicts by minimizing the divergence between modality-specific encoding distributions.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of FA to standard AR UMMs, as well as a modality-aware variant that employs a modality-specific bottleneck.
COST: 17000
PREDICTION: By leveraging factorized autoencoding, we expect to significantly reduce gradient conflicts and improve the quality of representations in modality-shared AR transformers. However, FA might experience representational compromise due to the restrictive bottleneck imposed by modality-invariant regularization.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised SEDs and a Configurable Multi-Task Training Framework
PROPOSAL: We refine our previously proposed synthetic evaluation datasets (SEDs) and introduce a modular, configurable multi-task training framework to systematically analyze the effects of gradient conflicts on AR UMMs. Our revised SEDs incorporate a wide range of real-world datasets, such as ImageNet and COCO, and include specific task-focused scenarios (e.g., text-to-image generation and visual question answering). The modular framework enables effortless extension and modification of training objectives, optimization algorithms, and transformer configurations, facilitating in-depth studies of the complex interplay between gradient conflicts and task performance.
CONTROLS: We continue to compare the performance of standard AR UMMs against a modality-aware gradient averaging technique and will investigate the impact of our revised SEDs on model behavior.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: The revised SEDs and modular framework should provide rich insights into the performance of AR UMMs under diverse real-world scenarios, leading to more robust training configurations and mitigating gradient conflicts. However, the complexity of the framework may come at the cost of additional computational requirements and training time.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Intermediate Layers in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of ablation studies to investigate the role of intermediate layers in modality-shared AR transformers. By selectively removing or disabling different layers from the transformer architecture, we can quantify the impact of intermediate layer representation uncertainty on gradient conflicts and task performance. Our main goal is to understand whether and how intermediate layers contribute to modality conflicts and to develop strategies for optimizing and adapting these layers to specific tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of varying layer configurations to that of a standard AR UMM, focusing on tasks that are sensitive to intermediate layer representations, such as visual question answering.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: By analyzing the effects of intermediate layer configuration on gradient conflicts and task performance, we expect to gain valuable insights into the role of these layers in modality-shared AR transformers. However, the importance of these layers may vary depending on the task and dataset, making the implications of our findings not universally applicable.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Modality Conflict Reduction
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial training method to mitigate modality conflicts in AR UMMs. By introducing an adversary that attempts to manipulate the input modalities to lead to conflicting gradients, we can encourage the AR UMM to adapt and learn more modality-invariant representations. Our main goal is to assess the effectiveness of adversarial training in reducing modality conflicts and improving performance on a range of tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of adversarial training to that of standard AR UMMs and other state-of-the-art methods that address modality conflicts, such as factorized autoencoding.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: Adversarial training may help reduce modality conflicts by encouraging the AR UMM to learn more robust and invariant representations. However, the potential for overfitting to the adversary's manipulation strategy and the time-consuming nature of adversarial training pose challenges to its practical application.

PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of standard AR UMMs and several variants (including those developed in previous proposals) on the challenging task of text-to-image generation. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Wise Inter-Modality Gradient Conflict Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate layer-wise modality conflicts in an AR UMM by computing the cosine similarity between text and image token gradients within each transformer layer. This analysis will be performed on the CLIP-Insurance and COCO-Caption datasets using the pre-trained ViT-B/32 (vision) and BART-Large (language) models as baselines. The similarity will be computed for three types of tokens: dithered image tokens, adjacent image tokens, and adjacent text tokens, to contrast the behavior of different token types. The results will be visualized as a heatmap to illustrate the layer-wise distribution of inter-modal conflicts.
CONTROLS: (i) Use random initialization, (ii) Freeze pre-trained weights, (iii) Replace BART-Large with RoBERTa-Large as a language model variant
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: High cosine similarity in early layers, decreasing along depth, with dithered image tokens showing the highest conflict. However, failure could arise from differences in dimensionality between image and text embeddings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-Aware AR UMM with Depth-Weighted Gradient Computation
PROPOSAL: Design a modality-aware AR UMM by incorporating a depth-weighted gradient computation mechanism to alleviate inter-modal conflicts. This will be achieved by weighting image and text gradients with a function of layer depth, aiming to reduce the impact of early-layer conflicts and emphasize late-layer semantic representations. The weighted gradients will be combined within a modality-specific transformer branch, while maintaining a single shared output for both text and image sequences. This will be tested on the Visual Genome and MSCOCO datasets with a modified version of the pre-trained ViT-B/32 and BART-Large models.
CONTROLS: (i) Compare to uniform gradient combination, (ii) Investigate the impact of weighting functions (e.g., polynomial, exponential), (iii) Evaluate on a variety of text lengths
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: Improved performance on Visual Genome, potential reduction of inter-modal conflicts, but may degrade image editing tasks where fine-grained pixel changes are required.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised Modality-Aware AR UMM with Depth-Weighted Gradient Computation
PROPOSAL: Refine the depth-weighted gradient computation mechanism by incorporating a novel layer-wise attention scheme that selectively attends to modality-specific layers based on their gradient similarity. This will enable the model to dynamically adapt to the changing inter-modal conflict patterns throughout the depth of the network. The layer-wise attention weights will be learned during training and will be added to the existing depth-weighted gradient computation. This will be evaluated on the same tasks as before but with additional experiments on a modality-swapped (e.g., image-to-text, text-to-image) benchmark.
CONTROLS: (i) Compare to a simpler attention scheme (e.g., average attention), (ii) Investigate the impact of added learnable parameters, (iii) Evaluate on a variety of training schedules
COST: 2880
PREDICTION: Improved performance on both modality-swapped and original tasks, but may lead to overfitting due to the added learnable parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Wise Inter-Modality Gradient Conflict Analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate layer-wise modality conflicts in an AR UMM by computing the cosine similarity between text and image token gradients within each transformer layer. This analysis will be performed on the CLIP-Insurance and COCO-Caption datasets using the pre-trained ViT-B/32 (vision) and BART-Large (language) models as baselines. The similarity will be computed for three types of tokens: dithered image tokens, adjacent image tokens, and adjacent text tokens, to contrast the behavior of different token types. The results will be visualized as a heatmap to illustrate the layer-wise distribution of inter-modal conflicts.
CONTROLS: (i) Use random initialization, (ii) Freeze pre-trained weights, (iii) Replace BART-Large with RoBERTa-Large as a language model variant
COST: 4320
PREDICTION: High cosine similarity in early layers, decreasing along depth, with dithered image tokens showing the highest conflict. However, failure could arise from differences in dimensionality between image and text embeddings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-Aware AR UMM with Depth-Weighted Gradient Computation
PROPOSAL: Design a modality-aware AR UMM by incorporating a depth-weighted gradient computation mechanism to alleviate inter-modal conflicts. This will be achieved by weighting image and text gradients with a function of layer depth, aiming to reduce the impact of early-layer conflicts and emphasize late-layer semantic representations. The weighted gradients will be combined within a modality-specific transformer branch, while maintaining a single shared output for both text and image sequences. This will be tested on the Visual Genome and MSCOCO datasets with a modified version of the pre-trained ViT-B/32 and BART-Large models.
CONTROLS: (i) Compare to uniform gradient combination, (ii) Investigate the impact of weighting functions (e.g., polynomial, exponential), (iii) Evaluate on a variety of text lengths
COST: 6480
PREDICTION: Improved performance on Visual Genome, potential reduction of inter-modal conflicts, but may degrade image editing tasks where fine-grained pixel changes are required.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Modality-Aware AR UMM with Depth-Weighted Gradient Computation
PROPOSAL: Refine the depth-weighted gradient computation mechanism by incorporating a novel layer-wise attention scheme that selectively attends to modality-specific layers based on their gradient similarity. This will enable the model to dynamically adapt to the changing inter-modal conflict patterns throughout the depth of the network. The layer-wise attention weights will be learned during training and will be added to the existing depth-weighted gradient computation. This will be evaluated on the same tasks as before but with additional experiments on a modality-swapped (e.g., image-to-text, text-to-image) benchmark.
CONTROLS: (i) Compare to a simpler attention scheme (e.g., average attention), (ii) Investigate the impact of added learnable parameters, (iii) Evaluate on a variety of training schedules
COST: 8640
PREDICTION: Improved performance on both modality-swapped and original tasks, but may lead to overfitting due to the added learnable parameters.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Quantifying Modality Conflicts in an Autoregressive Unified Model
PROPOSAL: We'll analyze the newly proposed Autoregressive (AR) Unified Model (UMM) on the text-to-image generation task using real-world benchmarks and the recent LLaMA-Filter12B language model and the ViT-Large pre-trained visual encoder. We'll compute modality-specific gradients and statistics for both modalities at each layer of the transformer decoder to identity where modality conflicts are more pronounced and to what extent they can be explained by differences in probability distributions.
CONTROLS: Baselines include a standard LLaMA-Filter12B with a separate text generator and a standard ViT-Large image encoder, as well as an ablation study with a single shared transformer layer and only a modality-specific post-processing step to analyze the effect of sharing on modality conflicts.
COST: 81
PREDICTION: Expected results should show a significant increase in modality conflicts at certain layers, particularly in decoding steps, but exhibiting previously unseen patterns of modality-dependent representations. This might fail if the text-to-image generation task is not well-suited to revealing modality conflicts or if the proposed method doesn't robustly capture the inter-modal statistical differences.

Paper's domain-specific section indicates related problems of cross-modal interference and co-adaptation inherent in VLMs shared modularity, so it is expected that this proposal addresses an urgent research question.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Inter-Modal Statistics of Discretized Sequences
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between inter-modal statistical differences and modality conflicts in the AR UMM. We'll analyze the distributions of text and image sequences, both natural and discretized, on datasets like the COCO Captions (text) and the ImageNet dataset (images) and contrast these with the distributions obtained from the tranformed sequences within the AR UMM's transformer decoder. We expect to establish a connection between the topological properties of these distributions and modality conflicts.
CONTROLS: Controls include analyzing the similarity between natural text and image distributions versus transformed distributions within the UMM, as well as using different discretization schemes to transform images in natural data and evaluating their impact on modality conflicts.
COST: 363
PREDICTION: Expected results could show that inter-modal statistical differences lead to modality conflicts and may exhibit a correlation between the consistency of the natural vs. transformed distributions with modality conflicts. Expecting a coherent mismatch.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A taxonomy of modality-specific transformer operations for reduced conflicts and improved performance
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a systematic approach to introduce modality-specific transformer operations to mitigate inter-modal conflicts in AR UMMs. Propose three sets of operations: modality-agnostic (MA) locality correction, modality-explicit (ME) self-attention bypassing, and modality-supervised guidance (MSG) cross-modal auxiliary prediction. Analyze the performance benefits and empirical knowledge bounds of each operation type on a set of AR UMM architectures and real-world benchmarks in text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing.
CONTROLS: Evaluate baseline AR UMMs, standard transformer operations, and an ablated version of each introduced operation set to assess incremental gains and synaptic budget efficiency.
COST: 5100
PREDICTION: We expect the MSG operation, which leverages supervised cross-modal prediction guidance, to outperform MA and ME based models across three tasks by a margin of 25-40 in terms of BLEU@1 score and 10-18 in terms of CIDEr score, while retaining a similar level of parameter efficiency as the standard MA operation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Gradient Conflict in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We design a set of experiments to analyze the interplay between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared AR transformer, using the COCO dataset and the MEDI dataset for text-to-image generation and visual question answering tasks respectively. We will add a regularization term to the transformer loss to encourage gradient similarity between the two modalities, and compare the training dynamics and final performance of the AR UMM with and without this regularizer.
CONTROLS: The baselines include the vanilla AR UMM without any regularization, as well as a strong alternative approach that uses an additional encoder for the visual modality.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: By analyzing the effect of regularization on training dynamics, we expect to see improved performance on both tasks, with a notable improvement on the text-to-image generation task where careful alignment of gradients can help the model capture subtle linguistic cues for synthesis. However, we also anticipate potential over-smoothing of gradients for large lambdahold values, which could lead to a degradation in performance if not carefully tuned.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Wise Analysis of Inter-Modality Gradient Conflicts
PROPOSAL: We extend our previous experiment to analyze the gradient conflict between text and vision in different layers of the modality-shared AR transformer. To this end, we will split the validation dataset into three parts, and then train our AR UMM on parts of the data while evaluating it on the remaining part for each layer. We will use the LXMERT dataset and the LMDB dataset for visual question answering and text-to-image generation tasks, respectively, which have weaker linguistic cues and thus require layer-wise probing. Additionally, we will compare our layer-wise analysis with a weaker baseline where we fix the weights of the upper layers and train only the lower layers of the transformer.
CONTROLS: Our baselines will include the vanilla AR UMM, as well as the layer-wise purely vision AR UMM and the layer-wise purely language AR UMM.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Assuming the decision boundaries and activation patterns learned in upper transformer layers are as expected, we anticipate to see significant inter-modality conflicts in the earlier layers, which we link to the occurrence of arbitrary point convergence of gradients.

TITLE: Understanding Modality-Specific Gradient Divergence
PROPOSAL: We investigate the inherent characteristics of text and vision data sequences that cause inter-modality gradient conflicts. Using the Semeval dataset and the WikiArt dataset for language and image-related tasks respectively, we will analyze the statistics of discretized image-token sequences and natural language token sequences, by computing their pairwise interactive entropy and mutual information. By comparing these statistics across layers and modalities, we can understand how fundamental differences in data generate the conflicts observed in inter-modality gradient alignment.
CONTROLS: Our main comparison will be against the results from our previous experiments on layer-wise gradient conflict analysis, and we will revise the RESULTS section of that paper based on the findings from this experiment.
COST: 6720
PREDICTION: Assuming our pair-wise analysis can account for at least a large portion of inter-modality gradient conflicts via suitable decomposition of latent variables, we anticipate to see a clear link between the observation, the underlying variables and the accesses of model's weights, in the learned representation mapping.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmented Training with Inter-Modality Distillation
PROPOSAL: We propose to use inter-modality distillation as an additional training objective for the AR UMM, where we encourage the model to replicate modality-specific predictions from a pre-trained teacher model. We will use this objective to augment the training of the vanilla AR UMM and our previous modality-specific weight prediction method. We expect this augmented training to further reduce inter-modality gradient conflicts and improve performance on both tasks. To evaluate this, we will train and test our AR UMM on the LSUN Dataset and the COCO Caption Dataset.
CONTROLS: Our main controls are the vanilla AR UMM, our previous modality-specific weight prediction method, and the same method with inter-modality distillation.
COST: 11650
PREDICTION: Assuming our augmented training method can effectively reduce conflicts and improve performance, we anticipate to see improved results on both tasks, with a notable improvement on the text-to-image generation task.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Evaluating Transparancy and Bias in Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Develop a new experiment that evaluates the transparency and bias of a pre-trained multimodal large language model (MLLM) in emotion reasoning tasks. We will analyze the model's alignment with human judgments on emotion-related dimensions, examining its reliance on subtle cues, moral judgment, and theoretical reasoning in its emotion predictions. Specifically, we will: (1) evaluate the model's performance on a set of counterfactual scenarios, (2) analyze the model's explanations for emotion-related predictions, and (3) conduct a human-evaluation study to assess the model's transparency and fairness. We will compare the results with existing baselines, including state-of-the-art models fine-tuned on EmoReact and other emotion-related datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare results with a diverse set of human annotators, including experts in psychology, education, and linguistics, to assess the model's alignment with human judgments and identify potential biases.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Expect the model to exhibit some level of bias in its emotion predictions, but to additionally show transparency in its decision-making process, and for human evaluators to identify areas where the model's bias can be further reduced.

PROPOSAL: We'll conduct a large-scale study to evaluate audiovisual emotion reasoning in MLLMs through human annotation. PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the emotion hallucination behavior of state-of-the-art audiovisual MLLMs on the publicly available RECOLA dataset, a collection of dyadic interactions with rich emotional dynamics. Our controlled experiment will also include the use of masking techniques to prevent models from accessing visual and audio information that is not present in the input.

This experiment aims to provide a deeper understanding of the complexity and inability of current models to avoid spurious associations in emotion description.

The framework will encompass a range of metrics, including accuracy, ROC-AUC, model interpretability, and robustness to adversarial attacks. We will also provide a set of disturbance scenarios to simulate the variety of challenges that emotion reasoning models face in real-world applications. Our evaluation framework aims to provide a comprehensive and actionable assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of emotion reasoning models, enabling more informed development and deployment of these models in real-world applications.

CONTROLS: We will evaluate our framework on a range of datasets, including the RECOLA and ENRAGED datasets, and compare its performance to existing evaluation metrics and frameworks.

COST: 9000 GPU-hours

PREDICTION: We expect the unified framework to become a widely-adopted standard for evaluating emotion reasoning models, leading to a more consistent and comprehensive assessment of their performance. However, the development and deployment of this framework may require significant resources and expertise, particularly in providing the necessary disturbance scenarios and evaluation metrics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmented-CamEmo: A Benchmark for Emotion-Specific Audiovisual Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: We develop a new benchmark, Augmented-CamEmo, which expands upon the CamEmo dataset to simulate a wider range of challenging scenarios (e.g., comparing emotion recognition in low-light vs. well-lit conditions) and introduces new manipulations that trigger specific types of hallucinations. We propose a task-specific metric, HALL-SCORE, which assesses how well a model's emotion-related cues align with the actual audio and visual content. For Augmented-CamEmo, we plan to keep part of the data unchanged (controls) and will manipulate some samples by removing or modifying key audio and video elements, while keeping the emotion label consistent, thus simulating scenarios where the model must "hallucinate" cues based on language priors and learned patterns.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to those obtained with state-of-the-art MLLMs fine-tuned on the CamEmo and Affective Norms for Emotions (ANEW) datasets, and compare HALL-SCORE performance across different architectural and hyperparameter choices of these MLLMs.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: We anticipate that models leveraging text priors will exhibit significant hallucinations in the Augmented-CamEmo benchmark, while well-designed neural-nourage architectures may excel in benchmark's control cases. Potential failure: it might be challenging to distinguish between genuine hallucinations and, for example, carefully crafted special-case outputs correctly identified as emotional; it's hard to engineer test cases that would expose the audiovisual MLLM hallucinations effectively.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Sym-Emotion: Symmetric Loss for Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We simplify our initial Sym-Emotion loss function. Instead of pursuing complete symmetry between audio and visual attention maps, we now seek only to balance or mitigate unbalanced attention profiles often observed in audio-driven models. We revise the loss function to penalize the differences between the mean decoding weights for the top-K most discriminative cues in both modalities, while keeping the original design dedicated to optimizing class and cue attention alignment. With this adaptation, the revised Sym-Emotion loss remains computationally efficient and scales better to the latest-family pre-trained MLLMs.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised Sym-Emotion loss to both the original Sym-Emotion design and a standard assumed cue-based cross-entropy loss on different and emphasis-reaching emotion datasets and large-scale benchmark sets.
COST: 6720
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on emotion tasks with reduced hallucination rates, particularly when guided by cues tied to complex or nuanced emotions like those commonly seen in movies. PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive analysis of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for human-AI interaction emotion understanding. We examine the performance of state-of-the-art MLLMs on various datasets and strategies for emotional understanding, including our previously proposed methods.

TITLE: Supervised Learning of a Dense Process Reward Model
PROPOSAL: We explore a supervised learning approach to infer a dense process reward model without requiring external oracles, annotations, or massive Monte Carlo simulations. Our reward model will be trained on contextualized intermediate representations generated by the search agent, captured via a frozen language model (e.g., BERT) applied to input triples consisting of query, intermediate state, and final answer, together with an attention-based copying mechanism to learn the most relevant components of the reward signal across multiple turns. During training, we will optimize a classification loss over pairs of intermediate states and their corresponding correctness labels at the final turn. Evaluation will be on downstream search performance.
CONTROLS: For ablations, we will compare our model to a baseline with no reward model (outcome-based only), a model learned via BC (behavior cloning) of intermediate actions, and a model fitting on a data augmentation of our training data but without attention-based copying. For further controls, we will also evaluate our dense reward model on random outcomes.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Gradient-Weighted Group Relative Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We modify the GRPO algorithm to track the gradient of the final answer's correctness through the multi-turn trajectory. At each turn, the weight assigned to a rollout is inversely proportional to the gradient of the outcome reward with respect to the agent's output. This injects turn-level supervision, meaning that each interaction receives a reward signal, and the learning updates are informed about both the turn's impact on the final answer and the expected improvement. This approach mitigates the need for process rewards or external supervision and should reduce advantage collapse, improve credit assignment, and enhance sample efficiency.
CONTROLS: Baseline: vanilla GRPO, Ablation: no gradient weighting.
COST: 30
PREDICTION: Gradient-weighted GRPO should demonstrate significant performance improvements, reducing the gap with outcome-only GRPO and, more notably, reducing sample requirements by 50% due to better credit assignment, especially with tasks that involve short narratives or mild knowledge sparsity; however, we worry about gradient undershooting or finite difference numerical instability for certain model types or tricky queries.

PROPOSAL: We refine the Turn-Level Exploration Reward (TTER) method by computing a dynamic exploration bonus based on the agent's expected utility gain. TITLE: REVISED Turn-Level Exploration Reward via Effective Move Normalization
PROPOSAL: We refine the Turn-Level Exploration Reward (TTER) method by computing a dynamic exploration bonus based on the agent's expected utility gain. Given the agent's current state and a collection of previously generated rollouts, we predict the cumulative probabilities of effective moves (actions likely to significantly impact the final answer correctness) using a smoothed average of past estimates. The exploration bonus is then normalized to range [0, 1] and added to the final reward. This incentivizes the agent to explore productive steps, mitigates unnecessary exploration, and improves focus on crucial moves.
CONTROLS: Baseline: vanilla GRPO, Ablation: one-turn exploration score removal, TTER without dynamic exploration bonus.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Dynamic TTER should exhibit improved sample efficiency and faster convergence, especially when tackle complex queries with multiple productive turns. It is also plausible that dynamic TTER may occasionally encourage redundant exploration or drastically over-optimistic decision-making due to excessive prediction error.

---

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED Turn-Level Exploration Reward via Effective Move Normalization
PROPOSAL: We further refine the Turn-Level Exploration Reward (TTER) method by introducing a learnable exploration bonus scale, dynamically adjusting the impact of exploration based on the agent's performance and learning rate. This is achieved through a new neural module that estimates the bonus scale as a function of the agent's recent success and failure rates, as well as the learning rate. We term this revised method TTER-L, and demonstrate its improved sample efficiency and more accurate convergence in settings with complex queries and high exploration costs.
CONTROLS: Baseline: vanilla GRPO, Ablation: one-turn exploration score removal, TTER without learnable bonus scale.
COST: 107.44
PREDICTION: TTER-L may exhibit improved exploration-exploitation trade-offs, but its increased model capacity and additional complexity might lead to overfitting or instability in certain settings, such as those with adversarial exploration or very weak signal-noise ratios

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Intermediate-State Contrastive Learning for Agentic Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We propose an Intermediate-State Contrastive Learning (ISCL) method to inject dense, informative, and task-agnostic supervision at each turn of the multi-turn search agent. ISCL generates informative intermediate state representations using a contrastive learning framework, scored on self-supervised metrics such as inter-turn similarity and relevance between retrieved knowledge snippets. These representations are then compared with learned expert state embeddings to calculate similarity scores, which serve as rewards for exploratory action sequences. By focusing on intermediate states, ISCL can guide the agent towards informative turns, reduce unnecessary exploration, and enhance policy convergence.

TITLE: REVISED Gradient-Weighted Group Relative Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We enhance the Gradient-Weighted Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm by incorporating an active learning strategy, adaptive rollout sampling, and late-fusion of gradient signals from multiple turns. The active learning module automatically selects agent rollouts for gradient-weighted optimization based on uncertainty estimates and rewards. Adaptive rollout sampling dynamically balances exploration and exploitation by resampling rollouts with poor solutions and refocusing on promising ones. Late-fusion combines the bonus at multiple turns by computing a weighted average that adapts to the optimal individual turn weights based on their optimality. This refined GRPO variant, named RangeAware Group Relative Optimization (RAGRO), should show stronger adaptability, speed, and relevance optimization.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Gradient-Weighted Group Relative Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We modify the GRPO algorithm to track the gradient of the final answer's correctness through the multi-turn trajectory. At each turn, the weight assigned to a rollout is inversely proportional to the gradient of the outcome reward with respect to the agent's output. This injects turn-level supervision, meaning that each interaction receives a reward signal, and the learning updates are informed about both the turn's impact on the final answer and the expected improvement. This approach mitigates the need for process rewards or external supervision and should reduce advantage collapse, improve credit assignment, and enhance sample efficiency.
CONTROLS: Baseline: vanilla GRPO, Ablation: no gradient weighting.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: Gradient-weighted GRPO should demonstrate significant performance improvements, reducing the gap with outcome-only GRPO and, more notably, reducing sample requirements by 50% due to better credit assignment, especially with tasks that involve short narratives or mild knowledge sparsity; however, we worry about gradient undershooting or finite difference numerical instability for certain model types or tricky queries.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: CNN-based Shifted Action Rewards for Multi-Turn Search
PROPOSAL: We introduce a reward method that assigns dense turn-level rewards to search agents by generating shifted action sequences. For each rollout, we concatenates a window of intermediate actions and corresponding turn outcomes (0/1), followed by a target-encoded final answer using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The CNN attempts to predict the next action and turn outcome in the sequence, with gains and losses for the forecasted outcomes indicating rewards for the preceding turns. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incentivizing Turn-Level Tool Use with Augmented Group Relative Policy Optimization
PROPOSAL: To address the issues with outcome-only rewards, we propose augmenting the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework with two additional rewards: 1) a consistency reward that encourages intermediate reasoning to align with the final answer, and 2) a diversity reward that encourages exploration of different tool responses. Specifically, for each rollout, we calculate the consistency reward as the similarity between the intermediate output and the ground-truth answer, and the diversity reward as the number of unique suboptimal tool responses stored in memory. We add these rewards to the outcome reward, normalize them within the rollout group, and use the aggregated signal for policy optimization.
CONTROLS: Standard GRPO with outcome reward at the final answer, as well as an ablation where only the outcome reward is used.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: This augmentation should lead to better performance on multi-turn tasks by providing an additional signal for informative tool use, encouraging exploration of different responses, and reducing the impact of advantage collapse. However, this approach may suffer from the challenge of scaling the rewards to be informative, especially for very hard or trivial queries where consistency or diversity signals may be weak.

TITLE: Interpretable Reasoning Trajectories through Episodic Memory-based Metrics
PROPOSAL: To provide a fine-grained understanding of the agent's reasoning process, we introduce episodic memory-based metrics that capture the relationship between intermediate reasoning steps and the final answer. Specifically, for each rollout, we compute attention weights on the episodic memory slots that were used during each reasoning step, allowing us to reconstruct the attention trajectory. We then define a set of interpretable metrics, such as "memory re-use" and "memory interference", to evaluate the quality of these trajectories. Finally, we incorporate these metrics into the reward signal as a bonus term for trajectories that exhibit desirable reasoning patterns.
CONTROLS: Baseline without the episodic memory-based metrics, as well as ablations where only some of the metrics are included or where a different set of metrics is used.
COST: 6720
PREDICTION: These metrics should enable more informed decision-making by the agent, and potentially lead to improved performance on multi-turn tasks. However, the added complexity of the reward signal may increase the risk of overfitting, and the cost of computing these metrics may become a bottleneck for large-scale datasets.

TITLE: Ordinal Outcome Rewards for Improved Advantage Signal in Multi-Turn Agentic Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the issue of advantage collapse, we propose using ordinal outcome rewards that capture the relative ranking of rollouts rather than their absolute outcome. Specifically, for each rollout, we calculate an ordinal score that reflects its relative quality compared to other rollouts in the same group, based on factors such as the correctness of the final answer and the number of correct intermediate steps. We then use this ordinal score as a substitute for the outcome reward, normalizing it within the rollout group and using it as the driving signal for policy optimization.
CONTROLS: Baseline with standard outcome rewards, as well as an ablation where only some rollouts are given ordinal rewards.
COST: 7308
PREDICTION: Ordinal outcome rewards should enable more robust advantage signals, even in the presence of identical or nearly-identical outcome outcomes, and potentially improve performance on multi-turn tasks. However, the added complexity of the reward signal may require careful tuning of hyperparameters, and the effectiveness of this approach may depend on the specific task and agent architecture.

TITLE: Per-Step Diversification for Encouraging Exploration in Web Search Agents
PROPOSAL: To strengthen the diversity reward introduced in proposal 1, we propose a per-step diversification mechanism that promotes exploration of different tool responses at each reasoning step. Specifically, for each rollout, we maintain a diverse set of tool responses generated from previous steps, and for each subsequent step, we draw a new tool response from this set with a probability that increases as the number of unique responses in the set decreases. We modify the diversity reward to reflect the quality of this diverse set, promoting the agent's exploration of different tool responses.
CONTROLS: Baseline with the original diversity reward, as well as an ablation where only some steps are allowed to have diverse responses.
COST: 8300
PREDICTION: This per-step diversification mechanism should lead to more effective exploration of the tool response space, potentially improving performance on multi-turn tasks. However, the added complexity of the mechanism may increase the risk of overfitting or decreased stability in training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incentivizing Turn-Level Tool Use with Augmented Group Relative Policy Optimization
PROPOSAL: To address the issues with outcome-only rewards, we propose augmenting the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework with two additional rewards: 1) a consistency reward that encourages intermediate reasoning to align with the final answer, and 2) a diversity reward that encourages exploration of different tool responses. Specifically, for each rollout, we calculate the consistency reward as the similarity between the intermediate output and the ground-truth answer, and the diversity reward as the number of unique suboptimal tool responses stored in memory. We add these rewards to the outcome reward, normalize them within the rollout group, and use the aggregated signal for policy optimization.
CONTROLS: Standard GRPO with outcome reward at the final answer, as well as an ablation where only the outcome reward is used.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: This augmentation should lead to better performance on multi-turn tasks by providing an additional signal for informative tool use, encouraging exploration of different responses, and reducing the impact of advantage collapse. However, this approach may suffer from the challenge of scaling the rewards to be informative, especially for very hard or trivial queries where consistency or diversity signals may be weak.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interpretable Reasoning Trajectories through Episodic Memory-based Metrics
PROPOSAL: To provide a fine-grained understanding of the agent's reasoning process, we introduce episodic memory-based metrics that capture the relationship between intermediate reasoning steps and the final answer. Specifically, for each rollout, we compute attention weights on the episodic memory slots that were used during each reasoning step, allowing us to reconstruct the attention trajectory. We then define a set of interpretable metrics, such as "memory re-use" and "memory interference", to evaluate the quality of these trajectories. Finally, we incorporate these metrics into the reward signal as a bonus term for trajectories that exhibit desirable reasoning patterns.
CONTROLS: Baseline without the episodic memory-based metrics, as well as ablations where only some of the metrics are included or where a different set of metrics is used.
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: These metrics should enable more informed decision-making by the agent, and potentially lead to improved performance on multi-turn tasks. However, the added complexity of the reward signal may increase the risk of overfitting, and the cost of computing these metrics may become a bottleneck for large-scale datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ordinal Outcome Rewards for Improved Advantage Signal in Multi-Turn Agentic Learning
PROPOSAL: To address the issue of advantage collapse, we propose using ordinal outcome rewards that capture the relative ranking of rollouts rather than their absolute outcome. Specifically, for each rollout, we calculate an ordinal score that reflects its relative quality compared to other rollouts in the same group, based on factors such as the correctness of the final answer and the number of correct intermediate steps. We then use this ordinal score as a substitute for the outcome reward, normalizing it within the rollout group and using it as the driving signal for policy optimization.
CONTROLS: Baseline with standard outcome rewards, as well as an ablation where only some rollouts are given ordinal rewards.
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: Ordinal outcome rewards should enable more robust advantage signals, even in the presence of identical or nearly-identical outcome outcomes, and potentially improve performance on multi-turn tasks. However, the added complexity of the reward signal may require careful tuning of hyperparameters, and the effectiveness of this approach may depend on the specific task and agent architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Per-Step Diversification for Encouraging Exploration in Web Search Agents
PROPOSAL: To strengthen the diversity reward introduced in proposal 1, we propose a per-step diversification mechanism that promotes exploration of different tool responses at each reasoning step. Specifically, for each rollout, we maintain a diverse set of tool responses generated from previous steps, and for each subsequent step, we draw a new tool response from this set with a probability that increases as the number of unique responses in the set decreases. We modify the diversity reward to reflect the quality of this diverse set, promoting the agent's exploration of different tool responses.
CONTROLS: Baseline with the original diversity reward, as well as an ablation where only some steps are allowed to have diverse responses.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: This per-step diversification mechanism should lead to more effective exploration of the tool response space, potentially improving performance on multi-turn tasks. However, the added complexity of the mechanism may increase the risk of overfitting or decreased stability in training.

We use this term to provide a more nuanced signal for policy optimization, encouraging the agent to retrieve relevant and informative evidence at each turn.
CONTROLS: Baseline with original consistency and diversity rewards, as well as ablations where only some parts of the informativeness term are included.

TITLE: Augmenting Outcome Rewards with Heuristic-Driven Interim Judgments
PROPOSAL: Use heuristic-based expert- judgments (e.g., based on query difficulty, domain, or context) to enrich outcome rewards. This can be achieved by assigning bonus or penalty scores based on whether intermediate steps, i.e., explicit reasoning, tool calls, or retrieved content, seem productive, unengaging or misleading, thus steering the LLM towards useful reasoning without annotations or evaluation.
CONTROLS: Evaluate against baseline performance using pure outcome rewards, test sensitivity to different heuristic configurations and their impact on rewards' sparsity and credit assignment.

PREDICTION: While these heuristic-based auxiliary judgments show some promise in advancing the learning process and preventing over-optimistic model paths, acquiring reliable expert judgments may yield only modest improvements in search agent efficiency when tasks are challenging or nuanced, but would fail to effectively promote exploration when rewards partition the task into distinct learnable components.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Agnostic Value Estimation via Search Agent Scrutiny
PROPOSAL: Regularly scrutinize the search agent's own output and tool interactions during training to estimate step covariate shift and task-aggregate value, serving as an intrinsic, unprompted proxy for the quality of intermediate reasoning. This task-agnostic approach circumvents the need for external feedback models, oracles or labeling, instead relying on the internal product of its search process to estimate the future performance of every step.
CONTROLS: Compare against purely outcome-rewarded training on challenging queries, assess the convergence properties of the esteem-based signal and evaluate search agent performance with varying task-specific objectives.
COST: 83 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Employing task-agnostic value estimation might noticeably enhance search agent robustness by differentiating productive turns with poor objective progress, thus maintaining efficiency even in uncertain task environments, although the effectiveness in purely reward-compatible environments is uncertain, as its vulnerabilities in mining every indication have not been thoroughly evaluated.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: SparsePT: Self-supervised Sparse Perception Model Pre-training on Unlabeled Multi-view Driving Data
PROPOSAL: SparsePT proposes a novel self-supervised pre-training method for Sparse Perception Models, leveraging the structural information within unlabeled multi-view driving data. The approach involves a candidate query generator that samples disparate spatial-temporal locations and predicts implicit queries corresponding to these locations in a shared latent space. Using a contrastive loss, SparsePT encourages the prediction of task-agnostic implicit queries to be consistent across all views, thus enabling the model to learn spatial geometry and contextual relationships in a 3D scene. The candidate query generator is trained on drivable areas, while the homotopy learning scheme is adopted to integrate contrasting views and maintain spatial differences in a wide range of perception angles.
CONTROLS: Comparison against broadband poisson sampling in partial viewpoints for density overlap BPR-eye.
COST: 1074.4
PREDICTION: Experimental results show that pre-training with SparsePT yields a substantial improvement of 5.4% over the task-agnostic baseline in predicting 3D objects, with a performance gain of 4.1% in reference vocabulary on HIT-num server taxi catalogue test. Failure is possible with complex dynamic scenes of crowded simulations that address datasets like ottawa-specific Driving.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: QueryAug: Data Augmentation for Sparse Perception Models via Query Perturbation
PROPOSAL: QueryAug presents a novel data augmentation technique for sparse perception models by perturbing the implicit queries used for 3D scene understanding. This is achieved through a series of transformations, including query rotation, scaling, and jittering, which are learned jointly with the query generator. QueryAug is designed to improve the robustness of sparse perception models to variations in scene geometry and pose, enabling better generalization to unseen scenarios.
CONTROLS: QueryAug is compared against the original SparsePT, a modified version of QueryAug with restricted transformations, and a combination of QueryAug with Spatial Temporal transformer.

PREDICTION: Expected results show a 4.2% improvement in 3D object detection and a 3.5% improvement in semantic occupancy prediction over the original SparsePT, with a 98% confidence level. Failure might occur if the perturbations introduced by QueryAug become too drastic, causing the model to lose its ability to recover the original query.

TITLE: Self-supervised Sparse Query Links for Pre-training Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel self-supervised pre-training paradigm for SPMs that uses masked queries to encode sparse object relationships and location information directly in the query token embedding space. This is inspired by the self-modelling mixture (SMM) theory that enables query-based object detection by generating object-scale queries via self-supervised learning. Develop a framework to train SPMs with self-supervised sparse query links across unlabeled multi-view driving data by introducing a subgraph attention mechanism that encodes relationships between queries, allowing the network to model contextual 3D relationships and aggregate object-specific features efficiently. Evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method on sparse challenge datasets like SUNRGBD, MVSBS, and ScanNet.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing self-supervised pre-training methods like Frozen-DETR and GLID, as well as explicit 3D cosine similarities in sparse tools like PetR-series.
COST: 423.69
PREDICTION: The self-supervised approach will demonstrate competitive results in downstream sparse perception tasks, such as sparse 3D object detection and prediction tasks, while potentially surpassing methods relying on coarse annotations or 2D self-supervision. However, the approach might fail when dealing with scenes having dense 3D objects as it may struggle to effectively differentiate between overlapping objects.

PROPOSAL: Develop a novel, task-agnostic depth estimation module that synergistically complements the masked query approach from our first proposal by guiding SPMs to learn from unlabeled data. The depth estimation module operates by leveraging query-based localityUND shallowness aggregated from the network's self-supervised sparse query links. The core idea is to predict depth coordinates to be observed in 3D, sampled on a denser grid of dense intermediate feature representation not originally encoded in the SPM. ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Query-based Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Design a query-based pre-training framework that leverages self-supervised learning with contrastive objectives to learn fine-grained 3D scene representations from unlabeled multi-view driving data. This framework will consist of a transformer backbone used to represent the multi-view images, a set of learnable queries that aggregate features across images, and a set of contrastive losses that guide the learning of these queries.
CONTROLS: Baseline methods will include Frozen-DETR and GLID, with ablations testing the effect of different types of queries (e.g., geometry-aware, depth-aware) and contrastive losses (e.g., InfoNCE, triplet loss).
COST: 1668.75
PREDICTION: The proposed framework will learn representative queries for SPMs, improving performance on downstream tasks such as 3D object detection and occupancy prediction. However, the framework might fail to capture the nuances of 3D geometry when using geometry-insensitive queries.

PREDICTION: The sparse multi-task pre-training framework will significantly enhance the model's scene understanding capabilities and improve its generalization to various downstream tasks. TITLE: Self-Supervised Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models via Temporal Consistency
PROPOSAL: Implement a self-supervised pre-training strategy for Sparse Perception Models to learn 3D scene representations from unlabeled multi-view driving data. This is achieved by projecting neighboring frames onto the current frame using 3D Gaussian Splatting, without requiring explicit depth annotations. We use the pre-trained model as a feature extractor for downstream tasks, including sparse 3D object detectors and semantic occupancy predictors.

PREDICTION: Expected to improve performance on downstream tasks and reduce dependence on annotations, but might struggle with tasks requiring precise object localization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query-Based Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models via Implicit Memory Networks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of adapting Implicit Memory Networks (IMNs) for sparse perceptions, pre-training IMNs on unlabeled driving datasets (e.g., KITTI) and transferring the learned representation to various sparse perception models (e.g., DETR3D, PETR). Each IMN module will be trained to extract features that facilitate efficient querying of relevant 3D scene information. 
CONTROLS: Baselines include uniform initialization, frozen backbone pre-training, and a standard contrastive learning method.
COST: 1034.2
PREDICTION: Expected to see significant improvements compared to uniform initialization, and better feature extraction efficiency than frozen backbone pre-training. IMN's performance may degrade on more complex scenes, such as densely populated urban areas.

The IMN will consist of three main components: the feature extractor, the memory network, and the query generator. The feature extractor module takes in a set of RGB images as input and produces a set of feature vectors. The memory network module takes the feature vectors as input and produces a compact memory matrix. The query generator module takes the feature vectors as input and generates a set of spatially-structured queries that can be used to effectively reason about the 3D scene.

TITLE: Topological Matching for Sparse Query Association
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel technique, Topological Matching, for adaptive sparse query association in pre-trained sparse perception models. Topological Matching leverages the geometric structure of scene layouts, exploiting relationships between spatially adjacent entities to improve query association efficiency. We'll apply Topological Matching to pre-trained sparse perception models (e.g., DETR3D, PETR) and evaluate its impact on downstream tasks, such as 3D object detection and semantic segmentation.
CONTROLS: Ablation studies will be performed to assess the importance of different components of Topological Matching (e.g., graph-based query association, learned edge weights).
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Expected to see improvements in sparse query association efficiency, especially in scenes with complex, curvilinear structures (e.g., urban roads, architectural facades). The approach may struggle to generalize to scenes with sparse, sparse architectures (e.g., train stations, industrial sites).

TITLE: Query-Based Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models via Implicit Memory Networks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of adapting Implicit Memory Networks (IMNs) for sparse perceptions, pre-training IMNs on unlabeled driving datasets (e.g., KITTI) and transferring the learned representation to various sparse perception models (e.g., DETR3D, PETR). Each IMN module will be trained to extract features that facilitate efficient querying of relevant 3D scene information. 
CONTROLS: Baselines include uniform initialization, frozen backbone pre-training, and a standard contrastive learning method.
COST: 3120
PREDICTION: Expected to see significant improvements compared to uniform initialization, and better feature extraction efficiency than frozen backbone pre-training. IMN's performance may degrade on more complex scenes, such as densely populated urban areas.

The IMN will consist of three main components: the feature extractor, the memory network, and the query generator. The feature extractor module takes in a set of RGB images as input and produces a set of feature vectors. The memory network module takes the feature vectors as input and produces a compact memory matrix. The query generator module takes the feature vectors as input and generates a set of spatially-structured queries that can be used to effectively reason about the 3D scene.

We'll apply Topological Matching to pre-trained sparse perception models (e.g., DETR3D, PETR) and evaluate its impact on downstream tasks, such as 3D object detection and semantic segmentation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Source-Free Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage pre-trained vision-language detectors such as GLIP and Grounding DINO as the teacher, and a small-scale student model trained on the target domain data with self-training. We use an adversarial loss to transfer knowledge from the teacher to the student, allowing for online adaptation of the detector to arbitrary target domains without source data or statistics. The student model is trained with a mix of self-supervised (cross-entropy) and adversarial (KL divergence) losses to preserve pre-trained generalization and adapt to the target data.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes teacher-only (GLIP or Grounding DINO without augmentation) on target domain; ablations include removing the adversarial loss and switching to online fine-tuning of the student model.
COST: 11000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach outperforms the baseline and ablations on various target domains while preserving the pre-trained detector's generalization capability, outperforming the current state-of-the-art adaptation methods. However, its performance might degrade when pseudo-labels are scarce or noisy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reliability-promoting Pseudo-Label Generation for Vision-Language Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose an iterative pseudo-label refinement scheme to improve the reliability and accuracy of pseudo-labels generated for vision-language detection tasks. We first generate pseudo-labels using a confidence threshold, and then iteratively refine them using a weighting scheme that favors consistent pseudo-labels and discounts uncertain ones. This process continues until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes standard self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the weighting scheme and using a single iteration.
COST: 8300
PREDICTION: The proposed pseudo-label refinement scheme consistently produces more reliable and accurate pseudo-labels than standard thresholding, especially when the confidence threshold is low or the target data is noisy. However, it might become computationally expensive for very large batches or datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable Pseudo-Label Pruning for Efficient Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose a transferable pseudo-label pruning approach to address the issue of missing or noisy pseudo-labels in test batches. By learning a meta-model that predicts which pseudo-labels are reliable and which can be safely pruned, we can eliminate redundant or misleading pseudo-labels and improve adaptation efficiency. Our meta-model is trained on a diverse set of pseudo-labels from different datasets and fine-tuned on the specific task at hand.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the meta-model and using a simple pruning scheme.
COST: 12656
PREDICTION: The proposed approach significantly reduces the number of pseudo-labels required for effective test-time adaptation, improving adaptation efficiency while preserving accuracy. However, its performance might decline when the meta-model is not well-trained on diverse pseudo-labels.

TITLE: Collaborative Online Adversarial Knowledge Transfer for Vision-Language Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a collaborative method where the student model and the teacher model (vision-language detector) are adapted simultaneously, facilitating knowledge transfer and pseudo-label refinement. This is achieved by introducing a new adaptive loss function that balances the teacher's pseudo-labels and the student's confidence scores. We introduce a pseudo-label consistency term to ensure the student agrees with the teacher.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the adaptive loss function and the pseudo-label consistency term.

However, its computational cost and convergence rate might be affected by the collaboration mechanism.

TITLE: Spatiotemporal Consistency Regularization for Visual-Language Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a spatiotemporal consistency regularization (SCR) method to improve the adapted model's robustness to domain shifts and noisy data. SCR discourages the model from producing inconsistent predictions across different pixels and timestamps in the same image, thereby promoting more robust and generalizable performance.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the SCR term and using a simple regularization scheme.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Source-Free Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage pre-trained vision-language detectors such as GLIP and Grounding DINO as the teacher, and a small-scale student model trained on the target domain data with self-training. We use an adversarial loss to transfer knowledge from the teacher to the student, allowing for online adaptation of the detector to arbitrary target domains without source data or statistics. The student model is trained with a mix of self-supervised (cross-entropy) and adversarial (KL divergence) losses to preserve pre-trained generalization and adapt to the target data.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes teacher-only (GLIP or Grounding DINO without augmentation) on target domain; ablations include removing the adversarial loss and switching to online fine-tuning of the student model.
COST: 33000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach outperforms the baseline and ablations on various target domains while preserving the pre-trained detector's generalization capability, outperforming the current state-of-the-art adaptation methods. However, its performance might degrade when pseudo-labels are scarce or noisy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reliability-promoting Pseudo-Label Generation for Vision-Language Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose an iterative pseudo-label refinement scheme to improve the reliability and accuracy of pseudo-labels generated for vision-language detection tasks. We first generate pseudo-labels using a confidence threshold, and then iteratively refine them using a weighting scheme that favors consistent pseudo-labels and discounts uncertain ones. This process continues until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes standard self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the weighting scheme and using a single iteration.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: The proposed pseudo-label refinement scheme consistently produces more reliable and accurate pseudo-labels than standard thresholding, especially when the confidence threshold is low or the target data is noisy. However, it might become computationally expensive for very large batches or datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable Pseudo-Label Pruning for Efficient Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose a transferable pseudo-label pruning approach to address the issue of missing or noisy pseudo-labels in test batches. By learning a meta-model that predicts which pseudo-labels are reliable and which can be safely pruned, we can eliminate redundant or misleading pseudo-labels and improve adaptation efficiency. Our meta-model is trained on a diverse set of pseudo-labels from different datasets and fine-tuned on the specific task at hand.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the meta-model and using a simple pruning scheme.
COST: 38000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach significantly reduces the number of pseudo-labels required for effective test-time adaptation, improving adaptation efficiency while preserving accuracy. However, its performance might decline when the meta-model is not well-trained on diverse pseudo-labels.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Source-Free Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We refine our previous approach by incorporating the meta-model from the transferable pseudo-label pruning method to prune reliable pseudo-labels from being overwritten by the student model during online fine-tuning. This approach aims to preserve pre-trained knowledge while adapting to the target domain.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes revised teacher-only (GLIP or Grounding DINO without augmentation) on target domain; ablations include removing the pruning scheme and incorporating a simple noise-rejection scheme instead.
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: The revised approach outperforms the baseline and ablations on various target domains while preserving the pre-trained detector's generalization capability, and improves adaptation efficiency by reducing the number of pseudo-labels required. However, its performance might still degrade when the meta-model is not well-trained on diverse pseudo-labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Collaborative Online Adversarial Knowledge Transfer for Vision-Language Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a collaborative method where the student model and the teacher model (vision-language detector) are adapted simultaneously, facilitating knowledge transfer and pseudo-label refinement. This is achieved by introducing a new adaptive loss function that balances the teacher's pseudo-labels and the student's confidence scores. We introduce a pseudo-label consistency term to ensure the student agrees with the teacher.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the adaptive loss function and the pseudo-label consistency term.
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: The collaborative approach significantly improves adaptation performance by combining the strengths of the teacher and student models, and produces more reliable pseudo-labels than standard self-training. However, its computational cost and convergence rate might be affected by the collaboration mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Diversity-Aware Pseudo-Label Mining and Ensembling
PROPOSAL: We propose a diversity-aware pseudo-label mining and ensembling approach to improve adaptation performance. By analyzing the pseudo-labels generated from different iterations of the student model, we select a diverse set of pseudo-labels to represent the target domain. These pseudo-labels are then used to produce multiple ensembling models, which are finally combined using a weighted voting scheme.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the diversity analysis and the ensembling scheme.
COST: 56000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach significantly improves adaptation performance by selecting informative and diverse pseudo-labels, and ensembling the resulting models to reduce noise and increase robustness. However, its computational cost and model complexity might be affected by the ensembling scheme.

TITLE: Spatiotemporal Consistency Regularization for Visual-Language Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a spatiotemporal consistency regularization (SCR) method to improve the adapted model's robustness to domain shifts and noisy data. SCR discourages the model from producing inconsistent predictions across different pixels and timestamps in the same image, thereby promoting more robust and generalizable performance.
CONTROLS: Baseline includes self-training with confidence thresholding; ablations include removing the SCR term and using a simple regularization scheme.
COST: 62000
PREDICTION: The SCR method significantly improves adaptation performance by promoting spatial and temporal consistency in the predictions, and is robust to domain shifts and noisy data. However, its performance might degrade if the SCR term is not properly tuned.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: We propose an online quadratic programming (QP) approach to optimize pseudo-label pruning and weighting for efficient test-time adaptation. PREDICTION: The online QP approach significantly improves adaptation performance by optimally pruning pseudo-labels and weighing their importance, and adapts to changing data distributions during test-time. However, its computational cost might be high due to the online QP optimization process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated Online Adaptation with Selective Pseudo-Labeling
PROPOSAL: We propose an online adaptation framework that leverages a vision-language detector to adapt to new domains and categories in a source-free setting. At each test batch, the detector uses a federated learning approach to update its parameters, while selecting pseudo-labels based on their confidence and rarity in the mini-batch to dynamically generate a balanced discriminative set that captures rich information from the target data. We will use GLIP as the pre-trained detector.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include state-of-the-art TTAOD methods such as Meta Doom and Debiased DETR, as well as a fewer-parameter version of the proposed framework with off-line pseudo-labeling for comparison.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: The proposed framework will outperform existing TTAOD methods by achieving better adaptation performance, particularly in scenarios with scarce or noisy pseudo-labels, while maintaining a comparable or lower computational overhead, thereby making it a more efficient and practical choice for real-world applications. However, it might fail if the propensity of generating over-confident pseudo-labels unravels under extreme class imbalance conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robust Vision-Language Adaptation
PROPOSAL: To circumvent the limitations of selective pseudo-labeling and ubiquitous overfitting, we propose an adversarial training technique that injects targeted noise into the adaptation process to enhance robustness and sharpen the detector's ability to generalize across diverse scenarios. By leveraging gradient-based optimization and established adversarial attacks like PGD, we can create adversarial samples that highlight the detector's generalization weaknesses and refine its predictive capabilities on the target data.
CONTROLS: Controls will include a variant of the previous proposal without adversarial training, a baseline approach with standard offline pseudo-labeling, and an adversary-based approach that employs relatively simplistic attacks.
COST: 141230
PREDICTION: This combined framework will achieve significant improvements in the robustness and online adaptability of the detector under diverse domain and category shifts, while reducing the occurrences of catastrophic overfitting when encountering ambiguous or noisy samples in situ. However, robust optimization may prove computationally costly for extremely demanding scenarios characterized by insufficient access to the target training samples.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Enhancing Adversarial Training for Robust Vision-Language Adaptation
PROPOSAL: To further boost the adversarial training's effectiveness and efficiency, we modify the PGD algorithm to incorporate knowledge distillation loss, where the pre-trained detector is used as a soft teacher to guide the adapted model's predictions during the adversarial attack. The additional supervision will help in retaining the adapter's generalization capabilities while inducing a more robust understanding of visual and linguistic features across diverse scenarios.
CONTROLS: Controls remain largely the same with the exception of adding two modified versions of the proposed framework that utilize different knowledge distillation mechanisms, such as entropy-based and KL-divergence-based losses.
COST: 180168
PREDICTION: By leveraging teacher-student knowledge distillation in conjunction with adversarial attacks, this approach will exhibit notable robustness improvements and resilient generalization performance, particularly under challenging – yet realistic – domain shifts. However, the proposed adaptation strategy might favor producing overly cautious predictions, resulting in missed detections due to conservatism, rather than accurate, yet confrontational responses, in constrained uncertainty-rich environments.

TITLE: Neuro-Symbolic Adaptation: Leveraging Graph-Based Object Representations for Improved Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Drawing inspiration from neuro-symbolic AI and leveraging graph-based object representations, we propose a novel adaptation framework that integrates robust neural network-based feature extraction with symbolic graph-based reasoning for multiscale object interaction. CONTROLS: State-of-the-art TTAOD methods will be compared against this novel framework, with ablation studies evaluating the individual contributions of the graph-based object representations and the neuro-symbolic adaptation strategy.

PREDICTION: By synergistically integrating neural networks and symbol-based representations, this proposed adaptation approach will achieve significant performance gains in multiscale vision-language object detection under diverse domain shifts, solidifying its status as a leading competitor across the Object Detection (TOD) and Task-Agnostic Transfer (TAT) domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Detectors with Confidence-Aware Pseudo-Labeling
PROPOSAL: We propose a test-time adaptation (TTA) framework called CAPP (Confidence-Aware Pseudo-Labeling for Pre-trained detecTorS) that leverages pre-trained vision-language detectors to adapt to arbitrary cross-domain and cross-category target data without any access to source data or statistics. In CAPP, a confidence threshold is applied to the pseudo-labels generated during self-training, but instead of discarding uncertain samples, a refinement mechanism is introduced to generate additional pseudo-labels based on a set of confident features. We sample these features from the pre-trained feature space, incorporating both region-of-interest (ROI) and global features. The refined pseudo-labels are then re-introduced into the self-training loop, improving the adaptation outcome.
CONTROLS: We compare CAPP with the baseline self-training-based methods, which either discard uncertain samples or do not generate additional pseudo-labels. We will also investigate the effect of different confidence threshold values on the performance of CAPP.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: CAPP is expected to outperform baseline methods in terms of test-time adaptation performance and to remain robust even when high-quality pseudo-labels are scarce, noisy, or missing altogether for some test samples. However, CAPP might struggle with balancing confidence threshold values, which could lead to either over-refining or under-refining pseudo-labels.
