ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Routing Learning for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment where we extend the MoE framework to learn routing policies across multiple tasks simultaneously. This involves training a shared routing network that can adapt to diverse task-specific requirements. Specifically, we train a variant of the fair Moisture-of-Experts model with an embedded routing predictor that learns to predict the task-specific routing policy based on the input data and the task labels.
CONTROLS: We compare against two baselines: 1) a model trained with a single-task routing policy, and 2) a model with a multi-task routing policy but without the shared routing network.
COST: 19678
PREDICTION: We expect our multi-task routing learning to improve the adaptability and transferability of MoE models across tasks, leading to better performance in a variety of downstream applications. However, this may fail if the shared routing network fails to generalize across different tasks, resulting in suboptimal routing policies for specific tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Revising Asymmetric Routing Loss for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We revise the asymmetric routing loss (Proposal 4) to incorporate a Threshhold-based noisy routing policy, where a random portion of the routing decisions are forced to switch, making it harder for the model to commit to a poor routing strategy. By fine-tuning the threshold and noise levels, we can control the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. Specifically, we modify the routing loss function of the fair Moisture-of-Experts model to include this noise injection component.
CONTROLS: We compare against the original asymmetric routing loss function (Proposal 4), and a baseline model with a completely random routing policy.
COST: 22680
PREDICTION: We expect our revised asymmetric routing loss to improve the exploration-exploitation trade-off of MoE models, leading to better routing policies in situations where a single good solution is hard to find. However, this may fail if the noise levels become too high, making it difficult for the model to converge to a stable solution.

PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment where we incorporate a hierarchical selection mechanism into the MoE framework, allowing for a coarse-to-fine selection of experts based on the input data's complexity and the task requirements. TITLE: Revising Pairwise Expert Regularization for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We revise the pairwise expert regularization term (Proposal 3) to add an additional filtering mechanism, where we consider only the top-k most similar experts for each token. This is done to alleviate potential over-penalization of experts that may still contribute valuable diversity, even if they are slightly redundant with their peers. Specifically, we use the popularity of each expert in the routing policy to determine their priority in the filtering mechanism.
CONTROLS: We compare against the original pairwise expert regularization (Proposal 3), and a baseline model that uses a uniform routing policy. 
COST: 45000
PREDICTION: We expect our revised pairwise expert regularization to better balance the need for orthogonality and diversity in expert representations, leading to improved performance and fewer cases of catastrophic forgetting. However, this may fail if the k-filtering mechanism becomes too aggressive and starts suppressing experts that might still contribute valuable knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Asymmetric Routing Loss for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment where we introduce an asymmetric routing loss function to guide the routing policy's adaptation to the data distribution. The loss involves two terms: one measuring the entropy of the routing distribution, and another assessing the alignment of the experts' diets with their corresponding representations. By controlling the strength of these terms, we can promote either random or structured routing policies according to the task's requirements. Specifically, we modify the routing policy of the fair Moisture-of-Experts model to incorporate this loss function.
CONTROLS: We compare against three baselines: 1) the vanilla fair Moisture-of-Experts model, 2) a model with a uniform routing policy, and 3) a model with a pre-defined routing policy.
COST: 62000
PREDICTION: We expect our asymmetric routing loss to improve the adaptability of MoE models to diverse domains, by optimizing the routing policy for the specific task at hand. However, this may fail if the routing loss is too late to commit to a structured routing policy, leading to suboptimal performance in tasks that require consistent routing patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Routing Learning for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment where we extend the MoE framework to learn routing policies across multiple tasks simultaneously. This involves training a shared routing network that can adapt to diverse task-specific requirements. Specifically, we train a variant of the fair Moisture-of-Experts model with an embedded routing predictor that learns to predict the task-specific routing policy based on the input data and the task labels.
CONTROLS: We compare against two baselines: 1) a model trained with a single-task routing policy, and 2) a model with a multi-task routing policy but without the shared routing network.
COST: 59000
PREDICTION: We expect our multi-task routing learning to improve the adaptability and transferability of MoE models across tasks, leading to better performance in a variety of downstream applications. However, this may fail if the shared routing network fails to generalize across different tasks, resulting in suboptimal routing policies for specific tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Revising Asymmetric Routing Loss for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We revise the asymmetric routing loss (Proposal 4) to incorporate a Threshhold-based noisy routing policy, where a random portion of the routing decisions are forced to switch, making it harder for the model to commit to a poor routing strategy. By fine-tuning the threshold and noise levels, we can control the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. Specifically, we modify the routing loss function of the fair Moisture-of-Experts model to include this noise injection component.
CONTROLS: We compare against the original asymmetric routing loss function (Proposal 4), and a baseline model with a completely random routing policy.
COST: 68000
PREDICTION: We expect our revised asymmetric routing loss to improve the exploration-exploitation trade-off of MoE models, leading to better routing policies in situations where a single good solution is hard to find. However, this may fail if the noise levels become too high, making it difficult for the model to converge to a stable solution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Expert Selection for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment where we incorporate a hierarchical selection mechanism into the MoE framework, allowing for a coarse-to-fine selection of experts based on the input data's complexity and the task requirements. Specifically, we use a recursive partitioning tree to classify input tokens into sub-groups, and select experts based on their relevance to each sub-group. This is implemented on top of the fair Moisture-of-Experts model.
CONTROLS: We compare against two baselines: 1) a model with a uniform expert selection policy, and 2) a model with a pre-defined hierarchical selection mechanism.
COST: 75000
PREDICTION: We expect our hierarchical expert selection to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of MoE models, particularly for tasks that require nuanced representations of complex input data. However, this may fail if the hierarchical selection mechanism becomes too rigid, leading to a failure to adapt to novel or unseen inputs.

ACTION: REVISE 2

PROPOSAL: We revise the progressive routing alignment mechanism (Proposal 2) to incorporate the hierarchical expert selection (Proposal 6) as a means to determine which experts should be adapted at each iteration. By selecting a subset of relevant experts to align with the input data, we can reduce the risk of catastrophic forgetting and improve the overall performance of the MoE model. PREDICTION: We expect our revised progressive routing alignment to improve the long-term stability and adaptability of MoE models, leading to better performance on complex and dynamic tasks. However, this may fail if the hierarchical selection mechanism becomes too restrictive, limiting the model's ability to adapt to novel inputs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Gradient-based Regularization for Expert Orthogonality
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a regularization term added to the MoE objective function to encourage orthogonality of the router's weight matrix. Specifically, we compute the pairwise similarity between each expert's outgoing activations (after routing) and measure its KL-divergence from an isotropic Gaussian distribution. This regularization term is added to the final loss during training.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Original MoE training without additional loss; Baseline 2: Adding a load-balancing loss as in standard MoE training; Ablation 1: Examining the effect of the regularization term alone without the load-balancing loss
COST: 1165
PREDICTION: We expect this experiment to mitigate some expert homogenization, as the orthogonality constraint should encourage routed experts to develop diverse, separate representations. The primary challenge will be finding the optimal strength of the regularization term, which may lead to under-specialization if set too low, or reduced performance if set too high.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized Orthogonal Routing for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We modify the standard routing mechanism by adding an additional regularizer to the load-balancing loss, which encourages orthogonal columns in the router's weight matrix. This should promote a diverse set of combinations of experts that are not overly dependent on one another.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard MoE architecture, an MoE with uniform usage regularization (a common variant of the load-balancing loss), and an MoE with an always-active shared expert.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: By encouraging orthogonal columns, the regularizer should improve the diversity of expert combinations, and lead to better language modeling performance, especially in cases where the input distribution is highly multimodal. However, it may also introduce additional noise in the training process, and require careful tuning of the regularization strength.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Expert Hierarchy for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose to organize the experts in a hierarchical fashion, where a subnetwork of experts is responsible for processing each token at each time step. The subnetwork is then composed of experts that specialize in different sequence positions or time steps. This should allow the model to capture temporal dependencies more effectively.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard MoE architecture with regularized orthogonal routing (proposal 1), a version of the MoE architecture with global routing (where the expert combination is determined globally for the entire sequence), and a sequence-level classification model that uses a single, shared expert.
COST: 1050
PREDICTION: This hierarchical organization should allow the model to better capture temporal dependencies and should be particularly beneficial for tasks that involve sequential reasoning, such as reading comprehension or mathematical reasoning. However, it may increase the computational requirements of the model, and may lead to diminished performance on tasks where temporal dependencies are not as strong.

TITLE: Adaptive Expert Pooling for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose to adaptively pool experts based on their performance, by routing tokens to the experts that have historically performed best on the current task or sequence. This should lead to improved performance by selecting the most effective experts for each task.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard MoE architecture, an MoE with regularized orthogonal routing (proposal 1), a revised MoE architecture with global routing and a fixed expert pool, and the revised temporal expert hierarchy (proposal 2).

PREDICTION: This adaptive pooling strategy should improve performance by selecting the most effective experts for each task, particularly in cases where the input distribution is complex and requires a range of specialized skills. However, it may also lead to overfitting or a lack of diversity in the expert pool if not carefully regularized.

TITLE: Multi-Objective Routing for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We introduce a multi-objective routing mechanism that balances the load-balancing loss with an additional objective that encourages semantic diversity among the selected experts. This is achieved using a bilevel optimization framework where the upper-level objective is to minimize task-specific loss and the lower-level objective is to encourage semantic diversity.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard MoE architecture, an MoE with regularized orthogonal routing (proposal 1), a revised MoE architecture with global routing and a fixed expert pool, the revised temporal expert hierarchy (proposal 2), and the adaptive expert pooling (proposal 3).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized Orthogonal Routing for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We modify the standard routing mechanism by adding an additional regularizer to the load-balancing loss, which encourages orthogonal columns in the router's weight matrix. This should promote a diverse set of combinations of experts that are not overly dependent on one another.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard MoE architecture, an MoE with uniform usage regularization (a common variant of the load-balancing loss), and an MoE with an always-active shared expert.
COST: 2100
PREDICTION: By encouraging orthogonal columns, the regularizer should improve the diversity of expert combinations, and lead to better language modeling performance, especially in cases where the input distribution is highly multimodal. However, it may also introduce additional noise in the training process, and require careful tuning of the regularization strength.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Expert Hierarchy for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose to organize the experts in a hierarchical fashion, where a subnetwork of experts is responsible for processing each token at each time step. The subnetwork is then composed of experts that specialize in different sequence positions or time steps. This should allow the model to capture temporal dependencies more effectively.
CONTROLS: We compare against the standard MoE architecture with regularized orthogonal routing (proposal 1), a version of the MoE architecture with global routing (where the expert combination is determined globally for the entire sequence), and a sequence-level classification model that uses a single, shared expert.
COST: 3150
PREDICTION: This hierarchical organization should allow the model to better capture temporal dependencies and should be particularly beneficial for tasks that involve sequential reasoning, such as reading comprehension or mathematical reasoning. However, it may increase the computational requirements of the model, and may lead to diminished performance on tasks where temporal dependencies are not as strong.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Temporal Expert Hierarchy for Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: We further revise proposal 2 by incorporating a feedback loop between the subnetworks at each time step. The output of each subnetwork is used to modulate the routing probabilities at the next time step, allowing the model to dynamically adapt to the sequence and capture long-term dependencies more effectively.
CONTROLS: We compare against the revised regularized orthogonal routing (revision of proposal 1), a version of the MoE architecture with global routing (proposal 2), and a sequence-level classification model that uses a single, shared expert.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: This feedback loop should enable the model to better capture long-term dependencies and adapt to the sequence more effectively, leading to state-of-the-art performance on tasks such as reading comprehension and mathematical reasoning. However, it may also increase the computational requirements of the model and lead to overfitting if not regularized properly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the impact of adaptive data augmentation
PROPOSAL: Employ an agent-based approach to dynamically update data augmentation policies $\mathcal{T}_{aug}$ during training, using reinforcement learning (RL) to adapt to the evolving distribution of labeled and unlabeled data. We will use the State-of-the-art transformers model MLM(RoBERTa) on the very large-scale real-world dataset ImageNet.
CONTROLS: We will compare against the current static augmentation policy of repeated flipping and rotation (Pretrained hub with-augmentation on image) as well as an ablation where data augmentation is kept fixed throughout the training process. As controls, we will also use 2 baseline changing of methodology that a static augmentation on pre-trained backbone + feature weighting during training.
COST: 3360
PREDICTION: We expect to see a 5% improvement in mAP on the validation set, with most of the gain coming from better handling of rare labels due to the adaptive augmentation policy. However, the performance might degrade with highly unstable adaptation, as the policy is heavily dependent on the exploration-exploitation trade-off.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint optimization of multiple training components
PROPOSAL: Use a bilevel optimization framework to jointly optimize the data augmentation policy $\mathcal{T}_{aug}$, the optimizer $\mathcal{O}$, the learning-rate schedule $S_{lr}$, and the loss function $\mathcal{L}_{loss}$. We will use the same model as proposal 1 and the same dataset ImageNet. Our goal is to optimize the entire configuration space using the bpps algorithm, focusing on an ensemble of jointly optimized methods rather than independent approach each component takes in current machine learning models. We also will use global optimal search strategy for both learning-speed, convergence speed as well specifics of our training behavior and trends.
CONTROLS: The proposed joint optimization framework will be compared to the current independent optimization approach for each component, as well as to proposal 1 which adapts only the data augmentation policy.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: By jointly optimizing multiple components, we expect to see a significant improvement in validation performance, with a potential increase of 8% in mAP, across multiple learning rate, tunning range. However, the optimization process may be computationally expensive due to the complexity of the bilevel optimization framework, and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid overfitting the training data.

TITLE: Investigating the impact of adaptive data augmentation
PROPOSAL: Employ an agent-based approach to dynamically update data augmentation policies $\mathcal{T}_{aug}$ during training, using reinforcement learning (RL) to adapt to the evolving distribution of labeled and unlabeled data. We will use the State-of-the-art transformers model MLM(RoBERTa) on the very large-scale real-world dataset ImageNet.
CONTROLS: We will compare against the current static augmentation policy of repeated flipping and rotation (Pretrained hub with-augmentation on image) as well as an ablation where data augmentation is kept fixed throughout the training process. As controls, we will also use 2 baseline changing of methodology that a static augmentation on pre-trained backbone + feature weighting during training.

However, the performance might degrade with highly unstable adaptation, as the policy is heavily dependent on the exploration-exploitation trade-off.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint optimization of multiple training components
PROPOSAL: Use a bilevel optimization framework to jointly optimize the data augmentation policy $\mathcal{T}_{aug}$, the optimizer $\mathcal{O}$, the learning-rate schedule $S_{lr}$, and the loss function $\mathcal{L}_{loss}$. We will use the same model as proposal 1 and the same dataset ImageNet. Our goal is to optimize the entire configuration space using the bpps algorithm, focusing on an ensemble of jointly optimized methods rather than independent approach each component takes in current machine learning models. We also will use global optimal search strategy for both learning-speed, convergence speed as well specifics of our training behavior and trends.
CONTROLS: The proposed joint optimization framework will be compared to the current independent optimization approach for each component, as well as to proposal 1 which adapts only the data augmentation policy.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: By jointly optimizing multiple components, we expect to see a significant improvement in validation performance, with a potential increase of 8% in mAP, across multiple learning rate, tunning range. However, the optimization process may be computationally expensive due to the complexity of the bilevel optimization framework, and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to avoid overfitting the training data.

ACTION: REVIS (2)
TITLE:  Joint optimization of multiple training components
PROPOSAL: Modify the bilevel optimization framework in proposal 2 to incorporate a regularization term that encourages the learned configuration to change smoothly over the course of training. Specifically, we will use an L1 regularization term on the difference between consecutive configuration updates. We also want to reflect higher complexity by suggesting various powerful methods.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Co-Fine-Tuning via Novel Multi-Modality Knowledge Wormholes for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We refine our framework for Co-Fine-Tuning via Multi-Modality Knowledge Wormholes by introducing a novel coupling mechanism between the multi-modality knowledge wormholes and the classification head. Our proposed mechanism, called Hydra, uses a neural network to learn a weighted combination of feature maps from different modalities, and then uses these weighted feature maps to inform the classification head. We hypothesize that Hydra will improve the effectiveness of the multi-modality knowledge wormholes by allowing them to focus on the most relevant features for each class. Controls will comprise comparing our refined approach with the original Co-Fine-Tuning via Multi-Modality Knowledge Wormholes framework.
CONTROLS: (a) Original Co-Fine-Tuning via Multi-Modality Knowledge Wormholes framework
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We anticipate that Hydra will significantly improve the performance of the multi-modality knowledge wormholes, especially in cases where the different modalities contain complementary information about the classes. However, if the different modalities contain duplicate or redundant information, Hydra may not improve performance and may even degrade it.

TITLE: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Selecting Adaptive Configuration Strategies in Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We develop an information-theoretic framework for selecting the best adaptive configuration strategy in multi-label image classification. Our framework, called ACSI (Adaptive Configuration Selection using Information theory), uses mutual information to measure the relationship between the training data and the model's configurations. ACSI identifies the most informative configurations and selects the best adaptive strategy based on this information. We will compare ACSI with existing static and adaptive configuration strategies on several multi-label image classification benchmarks.
CONTROLS: (a) Random search for selecting the best possible configuration; (b) State-of-the-art pre-defined augmentations with Adam optimizer
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We expect ACSI to outperform existing static and adaptive configuration strategies by selecting the best adaptive configuration strategy for the task at hand. However, if ACSI fails to capture the complex relationships between the training data and the model's configurations, it may select suboptimal configurations, leading to decreased performance.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Least-Informed-Based Hedging (LIBH) for Adaptive Learning Rates in Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We refine our LIBH algorithm by incorporating a novel regularization term that encourages the model to explore the solution space more thoroughly. This regularization term, called "Exploration-Exploitation" (EE), adds a penalty term to the objective function that promotes the model to explore different parts of the solution space. We hypothesize that EE will improve the effectiveness of LIBH by encouraging the model to find more optimal solutions. Controls will comprise comparing our refined LIBH algorithm with the original LIBH algorithm and with other adaptive learning rate methods.
CONTROLS: (a) Original LIBH algorithm; (b) Stochastic gradient descent with a fixed learning rate
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the refined LIBH algorithm with EE will outperform the original LIBH algorithm and other adaptive learning rate methods, especially in cases where the solution space is complex and high-dimensional. However, if EE adds too much noise to the objective function, it may degrade the performance of LIBH.

PROPOSAL: We refine our framework for Co-Fine-Tuning via Multi-Modality Knowledge Wormholes by introducing a novel coupling mechanism between the multi-modality knowledge wormholes and the classification head. We hypothesize that Hydra will improve the effectiveness of the multi-modality knowledge wormholes by allowing them to focus on the most relevant features for each class. TITLE: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Selecting Adaptive Configuration Strategies in Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We develop an information-theoretic framework for selecting the best adaptive configuration strategy in multi-label image classification. Our framework, called ACSI (Adaptive Configuration Selection using Information theory), uses mutual information to measure the relationship between the training data and the model's configurations. ACSI identifies the most informative configurations and selects the best adaptive strategy based on this information. We will compare ACSI with existing static and adaptive configuration strategies on several multi-label image classification benchmarks.
CONTROLS: (a) Random search for selecting the best possible configuration; (b) State-of-the-art pre-defined augmentations with Adam optimizer
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: We expect ACSI to outperform existing static and adaptive configuration strategies by selecting the best adaptive configuration strategy for the task at hand. However, if ACSI fails to capture the complex relationships between the training data and the model's configurations, it may select suboptimal configurations, leading to decreased performance.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Least-Informed-Based Hedging (LIBH) for Adaptive Learning Rates in Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We refine our LIBH algorithm by incorporating a novel regularization term that encourages the model to explore the solution space more thoroughly. This regularization term, called "Exploration-Exploitation" (EE), adds a penalty term to the objective function that promotes the model to explore different parts of the solution space. We hypothesize that EE will improve the effectiveness of LIBH by encouraging the model to find more optimal solutions. Controls will comprise comparing our refined LIBH algorithm with the original LIBH algorithm and with other adaptive learning rate methods.
CONTROLS: (a) Original LIBH algorithm; (b) Stochastic gradient descent with a fixed learning rate

PREDICTION: We anticipate that the refined LIBH algorithm with EE will outperform the original LIBH algorithm and other adaptive learning rate methods, especially in cases where the solution space is complex and high-dimensional. However, if EE adds too much noise to the objective function, it may degrade the performance of LIBH.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Configuration of Multi-Label Image Classification: A Dynamic AutoML Approach
PROPOSAL: This experiment aims to design and evaluate an adaptive configuration framework for the core training components of a multi-label image classifier. At the beginning of training, a budget is set for dynamic configuration ($B_{config}$). The framework iteratively samples configurations from a predefined search space, leveraging a joint optimization approach that considers the interactions among data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule and loss function as part of a multi-objective optimization problem, defined as minimizing empirical risk, regularization, and augmentation capacity.
At each iteration, a joint optimizer is used to maximize the validation performance, leaping until convergence or until the budget is exhausted. To manage the high dimensionality of the configuration space, we utilize a hierarchical, progressive search strategy (HPS2) that exploits gradual subset(proc) rules and but restructuring. This strategy starts with basic and progressively relaxes rules, leading to  variant and nuanced squat convergence at straight tech episodes.
Controls:
1. Baseline 1: Static configuration, fixed throughout the entire training process.
2. Baseline 2: Staged scheduling approach, where each component is tuned separately and independently during predefined milestones.
3. Ablation: Use one component at a time (learned augmentation policy with fixed optimizer, etc.).
COST: 607.5
PREDICTION: The proposed adaptive configuration framework will yield higher final performance and better handling of rare labels than static configurations, and would demonstrate superiority over staged scheduling in at least 90\% scenarios within 68% confidence interval.

 Controls:

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Progressive Additive Optimization for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: This experiment introduces a progressive additive optimization (PAO) approach that adaptively selects and incorporates relevant training components tailored to the evolving training state. PAO is divided into two stages: 1) additive search and 2) progressive selection. In the first stage, PAO identifies a pool of relevant components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) using a multi-objective optimization framework, considering their individual and joint contributions to the model's performance.
In the second stage, PAO progressively selects the most beneficial components from the identified pool, assigning them to the model across different training phases.
Controls:
1. Baseline: Using static configuration.
2. Baseline: Using staged scheduling approach.
3. Ablation: Using additive optimization without progressive selection (early stopping).
COST: 815
PREDICTION: PAO will achieve state-of-the-art performance for multi-label image classification, notably in handling rare labels and avoiding overfitting, by adaptively selecting the most relevant training components for the evolving training state, achieving 95% or above true accuracy rankings compared with competitive methods with prior adjustments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Training State on Adaptive Configuration Strategies
PROPOSAL: This theoretical study aims to analyze the impact of training state on the performance of adaptive configuration strategies (as previously proposed in components 1-5). We will investigate how different training states (e.g., early stages, convergence, divergence) affect the selection and adaptation of training components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) and how these changes impact the overall performance of the model.
Specifically, we will use a probabilistic framework to model the relationships between training state, adaptive configuration strategies, and model performance, allowing us to identify key factors that contribute to the success or failure of adaptive configuration methods.
Controls:
1. Baseline: Assuming a fixed training state with a static configuration.
2. Baseline: Assuming an average training state with a static configuration.
3. Ablation: Removing or replacing the probabilistic framework with a simpler or more complex model.
COST: 1584
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal that training state has a significant impact on the performance of adaptive configuration strategies, with optimal performance achieved when the model is in a state of moderate stability and adaptability, and will provide actionable insights for improving the design of adaptive configuration methods.

PROPOSAL: This experiment introduces a progressive additive optimization (PAO) approach that adaptively selects and incorporates relevant training components tailored to the evolving training state. PAO is divided into two stages: 1) additive search and 2) progressive selection. In the first stage, PAO identifies a pool of relevant components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) using a multi-objective optimization framework, considering their individual and joint contributions to the model's performance.
In the second stage, PAO progressively selects the most beneficial components from the identified pool, assigning them to the model across different training phases.
Controls:
1. Baseline: Using static configuration.
2. Baseline: Using staged scheduling approach.
3. Ablation: Using additive optimization without progressive selection (early stopping).

PREDICTION: PAO will achieve state-of-the-art performance for multi-label image classification, notably in handling rare labels and avoiding overfitting, by adaptively selecting the most relevant training components for the evolving training state, achieving 95% or above true accuracy rankings compared with competitive methods with prior adjustments.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 1
TITLE: Adaptive Configuration of Multi-Label Image Classification: A Dynamic AutoML Approach
PROPOSAL: REVISED 
This experiment aims to design and evaluate an adaptive configuration framework for the core training components of a multi-label image classifier. At the beginning of training, a budget is set for dynamic configuration ($B_{config}$). The framework iteratively samples configurations from a predefined search space, leveraging a joint optimization approach that considers the interactions among data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function as part of a multi-objective optimization problem, defined as minimizing empirical risk, regularization, and augmentation capacity.
At each iteration, a joint optimizer is used to maximize the validation performance, leap until convergence or until the budget is exhausted. To manage the high dimensionality of the configuration space, we utilize a hierarchical, progressive search strategy (HPS2) that exploits gradual subset spanning rules and subgroup restructuring. This strategy starts with basic and progressively relaxes rules, leading to nuanced convergence at a few pivotal learning episodes.
Controls:
1. Baseline 1: Static configuration, fixed throughout the entire training process.
2. Baseline 2: Staged scheduling approach, where each component is tuned separately and independently during predefined milestones.
3. Ablation: Use one component at a time (learned augmentation policy with fixed optimizer, etc.).
COST: 6732.5

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Training State on Adaptive Configuration Strategies
PROPOSAL: This theoretical study aims to analyze the impact of training state on the performance of adaptive configuration strategies (as previously proposed in components 1-5). We will investigate how different training states (e.g., early stages, convergence, divergence) affect the selection and adaptation of training components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) and how these changes impact the overall performance of the model.
Specifically, we will use a probabilistic framework to model the relationships between training state, adaptive configuration strategies, and model performance, allowing us to identify key factors that contribute to the success or failure of adaptive configuration methods.
Controls:
1. Baseline: Assuming a fixed training state with a static configuration.
2. Baseline: Assuming an average training state with a static configuration.
3. Ablation: Removing or replacing the probabilistic framework with a simpler or more complex model.
COST: 4752.5
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal that training state has a significant impact on the performance of adaptive configuration strategies, with optimal performance achieved when the model is in a state of moderate stability and adaptability, and will provide actionable insights for improving the design of adaptive configuration methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation Framework (AAF)
PROPOSAL: Implement AAF, a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework for adapting data augmentation policies, optimizers, learning-rate schedules, and loss functions over the course of training. AAF will use conditional actor-critic methods to learn to allocate fine-grained control over each component, while accounting for nonlinear interactions among components. AAF will be trained on a combination of real-world datasets (eg, PASCAL VOC, COCO), and used to adapt on a separate set of validation and test images from the same datasets.
CONTROLS: 
  1. Baseline AAF without MARL, using single dynamic strategies (e.g., constant learning rate, rotation augmentation, focal loss) which are still learned during training and dynamically updated per epoch (our grid search baseline inspires this line of experimentation);
  2. Several state-of-the-art static augmentation and optimizer baselines (e.g., CutMix, AutoAugment, Adam with cosine schedule);
  3. Offline, state-of-the-art configuration search methods (e.g., Bayesian optimization, random search with clustered models of the performance landscape).
COST: 80
PREDICTION: AAF will outperform the static baselines by 2-5%, while converging faster than baseline AAF and handling rare labels better. However, it still might struggle with extreme cases of data imbalance or with overlapping augmentation and optimization steps, potentially impacting its efficiency and optimization stability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Hyperparameter Tuning w/ Bayesian Optimization (OHT-BO)
PROPOSAL: Implement an online, Bayesian optimization method, specifically an Expected Improvement (EI) criterion, to adaptively select hyperparameters from a shared search space for multiple components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, loss function) during training. By continuously evaluating the performance gain of new hyperparameter sets on a validation set and computing the corresponding expected improvement, OHT-BO will iteratively select the most promising hyperparameter set, making adjustments throughout training without requiring precomputation or additional eval steps. We'll evaluate its effectiveness on the PASCAL VOC and COCO datasets.
CONTROLS:
  1. Static hyperparameter tuning (using a single, fixed set of hyperparameters for all training iterations, with Bayesian optimization serving as the offline search method);
  2. OHT with random search instead of EI;
  3. Adaptive augmentation framework baseline from previous proposal.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: OHT-BO should enhance the adaptive capability of static components during training, outperforming the AAF for no fixed strategy usage conditions and coping with deployment latencies where parallel CPUs do not interact (showing where OHT-BO and AAF can't effortlessly reach coordination for particular deployment schedules).

PROPOSAL: Revise the Co-Adaptive Component Tuning approach to utilize a multi-stage framework that jointly and cooperatively adapts the individual components of a multi-label classification model in a hierarchical manner. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Dynamic Optimization of Core Training Components for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel adaptive optimization framework, dubbed Hydra, which jointly learns the data augmentation strategy, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function in a dynamic and interactively coordinated manner over the course of training. Hydra's core innovation lies in a recursive uncertainty estimation procedure that estimates the uncertainty of each component's performance and learning schedule, enabling the remaining components to adapt their behavior on the fly. We apply Hydra to the Microsoft COCO and Imagenet subset datasets, using the mean average precision (MAP) metric and evaluating the impact of joint optimization on label imbalances, and stability and convergence rates.
CONTROLS: We compare Hydra against a suite of baselines, including a random search over the entire configuration space and a staged scheduling approach where each component is optimized individually in a pre-specified sequence.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Hydra should exhibit superior performance across various evaluation metrics and improve convergence stability compared to static configuration baselines, while reducing the need for manual hyperparameter tuning. However, the framework's complexity might lead to occasional decreases in performance during the early stages of training, depending on its initial uncertainty estimates.

TITLE: Inter-Component Regularization for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a regularization-based approach to simplify the joint optimization problem of Hydra. By introducing a set of inter-component regularization terms that promote cooperation and orthogonality among the training components, we reduce the complexity of the optimization problem and accelerate the convergence of Hydra. TITLE: Debiasing Hydra for Class Imbalance
PROPOSAL: We address the issue of class imbalance in Hydra by introducing a novel debiasing technique that adaptively reweights the training samples to ensure a more balanced distribution of labels. This is achieved through the use of an attention mechanism that focuses on the minority classes during training, thereby mitigating the impact of the majority classes on the optimization process.
CONTROLS: We compare our debiasing approach against the original Hydra framework, as well as a variant without debiasing, and a state-of-the-art class-balancing technique.

However, the added computation required for debiasing might slow down the framework, and the effectiveness of the debiasing mechanism depends on the specific imbalanced distribution of the dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantization-aware Transformer Training with Domain Adversarial Regularization
PROPOSAL: We design a novel approach that combines post-training quantization with a domain adversarial regularization (DAR) term in the training loss. This term encourages the learned quantization boundaries to be more robust to outliers and better capture the underlying semantic space, while the calibration set is still small and limited. The DAR term incentivizes the model to focus on features shared across different views, rather than being overly specialized to a specific calibration sample.
CONTROLS: Compare to PTQ with standard calibration set and No Dar PTQ with increased calibration set size as in UQR.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Quantization accuracy will be significantly improved compared to standard post-training quantization, but we expect performance to degrade ever so slightly compared to standard 32-bit training with high-quality calibration sets, mainly due to information loss in the quantization process, with potential for further improvement through finer calibration and tuning of DAR. 

The idea is to leverage gradient-based calibration of quantization, but directly optimizing it in an adversarial manner. The specific instantiations of the idea are experimental engineering. 

(DAR objective minimizes Clien and optimizer equilibrium between real parameterization, projected onto desired LQ, and the equivalent loss over PWQ parameterizations.)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Calibration Set Aggregation using Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We propose a graph neural network (GNN) based approach to aggregate multiple calibration sets from diverse scenes to create a pooled calibration set. The GNN takes the calibration samples from different scenes as nodes and constructs a graph based on their similarity in latent space. It then aggregates the calibration samples by attending to the graph and weighting samples based on their relevance. This approach allows us to create a rich and diverse pooled calibration set that can capture the major part of the expected data distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard PTQ with a single calibration set, PTQ with multiple unaggregated calibration sets, and proposed auto-scaling bitwidth approach with a single calibration set.
COST: 11700
PREDICTION: Significant improvement in quantization accuracy (up to 7%) compared to standard PTQ with a single calibration set, and up to 3% compared to PTQ with multiple unaggregated calibration sets, due to the creation of a more diverse and representative pooled calibration set. However, performance might degrade slightly (up to 1%) compared to PTQ with a single calibration set that is very representative of the test distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Quantization Ranges for Data-Independent Tokens
PROPOSAL: Analyze the activation statistics of camera and register tokens in VGGT to identify patterns of heavy-tailing and high variance. Develop a "'influence function" approach to measure the relative impact of each token on the overall quantization range and devise an adaptive clipping scheme that dynamically adjusts the quantization range based on token influence. Evaluate the adaptive clipping scheme on the SUN3D, ScanNet and MatterPort3D datasets for dense depth estimation and camera pose estimation.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard quantization schemes (uniform and learned quantization) and VGGT with full precision
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive filtering approach can identify and mitigate extreme variance in data-independent tokens, but its effectiveness may suffer on very large scenes or aggression in extreme conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automatic Generation of Diverse Calibration Sets using Rademacher Complexity
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to generate a diverse set of calibration samples using techniques inspired by empirical Rademacher complexity. This approach aims to capture the variability and representativeness of the 3D scene distribution. Evaluate the automatic calibration set generator on the Renders, ScanNet and SUN3D datasets for camera pose estimation and point map regression.
CONTROLS: Compare against manually selected calibration sets and VGGT with full precision
COST: 330 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Rademacher Complexity based generator may create diverse sets but requires validation of calibration statistics in practical usage scenarios, as well as potentially trade-off between diversity and calibration size limitations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Automatic Generation of Diverse Calibration Sets using Rademacher Complexity
PROPOSAL: Modify the approach from turn 2 to utilize a transfer learning method that leverages pre-trained models to learn a data distribution over the calibration set. This can be achieved by fine-tuning a pre-trained VGGT model on a small subset of scenes and leveraging the learned representation to generate diverse calibration samples. Evaluate the transfer learning approach on the Renders and ScanNet datasets for point map regression and camera pose estimation.
CONTROLS: Compare against manually selected calibration sets and standard VGGT with full precision
COST: 495 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The transfer learning approach may introduce domain adaptation challenges on diverse scenes and could indeed leverage the pre-trained model to generate representative data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantization-Aware Training for VGGT with Partial Precision Activations
PROPOSAL: Propose a technique for quantization-aware training (QAT) that supports partial precision activations, where some activations are kept at full precision while others are quantized. This approach aims to preserve the information in the high-variance data-independent tokens while reducing the precision of activations with lower sensitivity. Evaluate the partial precision QAT approach on the ScanNet, SUN3D, and MatterPort3D datasets for camera pose estimation and point map regression.
CONTROLS: Compare against VGGT with full precision, post-training quantization, and standard quantization schemes
COST: 720 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The partial precision QAT approach may mitigate the loss of information in activations with heavy tails, but requires careful tuning of the precision levels and could lead to increased computational costs during training.

PROPOSAL: Further modify the approach from turn 2 by introducing an uncertainty estimation module to evaluate the confidence of the generated calibration samples. This module can reject samples that are outliers or have low confidence, resulting in a more representative and diverse calibration set. Evaluate the uncertainty estimation module on the Renders and ScanNet datasets for point map regression and camera pose estimation.
CONTROLS: Compare against manually selected calibration sets, standard VGGT with full precision, and transfer learning approach (introduced in turn 4)
COST: 930 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The uncertainty estimation module may indeed improve the quality of the generated calibration set, but requires careful tuning of the rejection threshold and could lead to a significant increase in computational cost.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Calibration via Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Propose a multi-task learning approach that utilizes knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from a full-precision VGGT model to a low-precision VGGT model. The full-precision model will be trained on a multi-task objective that includes tasks such as camera pose estimation, point map regression, and dense depth estimation. The low-precision model will be trained on a distilled version of the multi-task objective, which aims to preserve the key information and relationships between the tasks. Evaluate the multi-task calibration approach on the ScanNet, SUN3D, and MatterPort3D datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare against VGGT with full precision, post-training quantization, and standard quantization schemes
COST: 1080 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-task calibration approach may effectively transfer knowledge from the full-precision model to the low-precision model, but requires careful tuning of the distillation temperature and could lead to increased computational costs during training.

PROPOSAL: Propose a label smoothing technique specifically designed for 3D reconstruction tasks, which takes into account the quantization effects on the model's outputs. Evaluate the quantization-aware label smoothing approach on the ScanNet, SUN3D, and MatterPort3D datasets for camera pose estimation and point map regression.

PREDICTION: The quantization-aware label smoothing approach may effectively improve the model's robustness to quantization errors, but requires careful tuning of the smoothing factor and could lead to a trade-off between accuracy and robustness.

PROPOSAL: Propose a generative adversarial network (GAN) approach to synthesize high-quality calibration sets for VGGT. ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Investigating the Effects of Different Calibration Set Sizes on Quantization Accuracy 
PROPOSAL: We will train the VGGT model using 10 different calibration set sizes (e.g., 100, 500, 1000 samples) and evaluate its performance on a real-world benchmark dataset, such as DTU-MultiView or D-u-VS, and a synthetic dataset, such as the heads dataset. We will assess the model's ability to generalize to unseen scenes and identify the optimal calibration set size that balances generalization performance and training cost. 
CONTROLS: Compare the 1.2B parameter full-precision VGGT against a PTQ-quantized VGGT with 8-bit weights and activations for all 10 calibration set sizes, without adaptive weights and static registers. 
COST: 336
PREDICTION: We expect a clear trend of increasing generalization performance with calibration set size, with diminishing returns beyond a certain point. PTQ-quantized VGGT should still underperform the full-precision model but the gap may decrease with optimal calibration set size.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Regularizing Activation Statistics for Special Tokens with Gaussian Process Regression 
PROPOSAL: We will incorporate a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) module to regularize the heavy-tailed, high-variance activation statistics associated with the data-independent special tokens. The GPR module takes as input the activation statistics and generates a Gaussian process that captures their underlying patterns, allowing us to predict the distribution of activation values. 
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the PTQ-quantized VGGT with and without GPR regularization on the calibration set and an unseen test set. We will also compare against baseline quantization methods that do not account for the special tokens' statistics. 
COST: 830
PREDICTION: GPR regularization should significantly improve the quantization accuracy of the special tokens, reducing errors and improving the overall performance of the PTQ-quantized VGGT. However, the effectiveness of GPR regularization may depend on the choice of kernel and hyperparameters.

TITLE: Experimental Evaluation of Standard Quantization Approaches on VGGT
PROPOSAL: Compare state-of-the-art post-training quantization methods including PTQ4ViT, GPTQ, and SmoothQuant on the VGGT model to determine which method yields the most accurate results in terms of camera pose, point map regression, and point cloud reconstruction under realistic real-world settings.
CONTROLS: Baselines should include full-precision VGGT, as well as uniformly quantized (all weights to the same precision), and "hardware-noise" quantized versions (simulating quantization limits of target hardware); calibrating methods should also be compared to naive uniform quantization with a single quantization step.

PREDICTION: Given VGGT's massive scale and sensitivity to quantization, state-of-the-art methods like PTQ4ViT and SmoothQuant should maintain high performance, while standard GPTQ may struggle due to its smaller calibration set; however, it may still outperform naive/incremental methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating DPT-style In-Context Learners on Synthetic Multi-Domain Tasks
PROPOSAL: Train a Decision Pretrained Transformer (DPT) on a synthetic multi-domain dataset, specifically a collection of robot manipulation tasks, each with distinct MDP structures and observation/action spaces. Evaluate its performance on unseen tasks within the same domain and across different domains.
CONTROLS: Train a Transformer-based policy from scratch on each task, use Algorithm Distillation (AD) as an ablation, and compare against a DPT variant with a reduced capacity (half the number of layers or tokens).
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: DPT will demonstrate strong in-context learning capabilities, matching or exceeding the performance of-policy-from-scratch approaches, but might require finetuning when adapting to unseen tasks. AD might slightly outperform DPT in certain scenarios, while the reduced-capacity DPT variant might show degraded performance.

Can scale DPT to diverse continuous-control settings and transfer its learning capabilities across different domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating DPT-style In-Context Learners on Synthetic Multi-Domain Tasks
PROPOSAL: Train a Decision Pretrained Transformer (DPT) on a synthetic multi-domain dataset, specifically a collection of robot manipulation tasks, each with distinct MDP structures and observation/action spaces. Evaluate its performance on unseen tasks within the same domain and across different domains.
CONTROLS: Train a Transformer-based policy from scratch on each task, use Algorithm Distillation (AD) as an ablation, and compare against a DPT variant with a reduced capacity (half the number of layers or tokens).
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: DPT will demonstrate strong in-context learning capabilities, matching or exceeding the performance of-policy-from-scratch approaches, but might require finetuning when adapting to unseen tasks. AD might slightly outperform DPT in certain scenarios, while the reduced-capacity DPT variant might show degraded performance.

Can scale DPT to diverse continuous-control settings and transfer its learning capabilities across different domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Action Distribution Modeling for Multi-Modal Continuous Actions
PROPOSAL: Explore different action distribution models, such as normalizing flows, conditional normalizing flows, and continuous action distributions conditioned on the task representation, to capture complex, multi-modal continuous action posteriors. Evaluate their ability to allow native action sampling at inference time and preserve the agent's interpretation as posterior sampling.
CONTROLS: Use vanilla DPT as a baseline, and ablate the different action distribution models in isolation to understand their contributions to performance.
COST: 2187
PREDICTION: One of the proposed action distribution models will significantly outperform vanilla DPT on tasks that require complex, multi-modal action spaces, but might come at the cost of increased computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Prompt Engineering for In-Context Policy Correction and Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Design a set of prompts that inject task-specific information about the observed state and reward structure into the agent during inference, aiming to directly correct and adapt its policy to the actual environment without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Evaluate the performance of DPT with these prompts in adapting to unseen tasks and parametric variations of known environments.
CONTROLS: Use the same DPT variant as in proposal 1, and ablate the effects of the prompts by removing them from the inference process.
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: The designed prompts will improve DPT's ability to adapt to unseen tasks and parametric variations of known environments, but might require careful tuning of the prompt synthesis process to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Robust In-Context Adaption
PROPOSAL: Train a DPT variant on multiple tasks simultaneously, using a shared task representation and separate action distributions for each task. Evaluate its performance on adapting to unseen tasks and parametric variations of known environments, as well as its robustness to concept drift and distribution shift across tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare against training DPT on individual tasks, as well as against a similar multi-task learning setup using AD as the policy backbone.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: The multi-task DPT variant will demonstrate improved robustness to concept drift and distribution shift, as well as enhanced ability to adapt to unseen tasks, but might experience decreased performance on individual tasks due to the shared task representation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Refining In-Context Policy Correction and Adaptation
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Introduce an iterative process to the prompt engineering proposal, where the agent not only receives task-specific information, but also its own previous actions and their consequences. This allows the agent to refine its policy correction and adaptation process based on its own exploration history. Evaluate the performance of DPT with this iterative process in adapting to unseen tasks and parametric variations of known environments.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original prompt engineering proposal, and against a baseline where the agent only receives task-specific information without any access to its own exploration history.
COST: 4980
PREDICTION: The iterative prompt engineering process will lead to improved policy correction and adaptation capabilities, allowing DPT to more effectively adapt to unseen tasks and parametric variations of known environments.

CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where DPT learns purely from its own exploration, as well as against a variant of AD that incorporates offline demonstrations.

PREDICTION: Incorporating offline demonstrations will improve DPT's adaptation capabilities, especially in environments with complex reward structures or where exploration is difficult. However, the performance improvements may be dependent on the quality and relevance of the demonstrations.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating the Scalar End-to-End Continuation Objective for DPT
PROPOSAL: We will explore a modified scalar end-to-end continuation objective for DPT to encourage exploration during in-context learning. Specifically, we will replace DPT's current supervised learning target with a mixture of the environment's return and a novel entropy-based reward term, where the return is estimated using sampled rollouts. The novel term encourages the model to maintain high entropy in the action distribution, enabling exploration and adaptation.
CONTROLS: Baselines will include DPT with its original objective, DPT with an additional entropy regularizer, and AD for comparison. We will also ablate the effect of the new entropy-based reward term by training DPT without it.
COST: 166.875 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to observe improved exploration and adaptation in DPT with the new scalar end-to-end continuation objective, particularly in tasks with complex dynamics or hidden states where online adaptation is essential. This could fail if the model's exploration becomes too aggressive, leading to over-discounted returns or poor policy optimization in tasks with different time horizons.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Enabling Continuous Action Modelling in DPT using Stochastic Gradient Normalized Parameterization
PROPOSAL: We will extend DPT to model continuous action distributions by approximating the posterior action distribution using stochastic gradient Normalized Parameterization (SNP). SNP combines the benefits of reparameterization tricks and the robustness of truncated normalizations, enabling efficient sampling of continuous actions while preserving the interpretability of DPT as posterior sampling.
CONTROLS: We will compare DPT with SNP to vanilla DPT and AD in terms of its ability to handle tasks with complex action spaces and its sample efficiency. We will also ablate the effect of SNP by comparing it to a reparameterization variant with the same normalization strategy.
COST: 368 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect DPT with SNP to outperform its ablated and baseline counterparts in tasks with high-dimensional and complex action spaces, where sampling and exploration are crucial. This may fail if the model's SNP approximation leads to oversmoothing or underutilization of the action space.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Very Deep DPT Models for Multi-Domain Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: We will investigate using very deep DPT models, with over 100 layers, as a means to improve the representation capabilities of DPT for handling diverse, complex tasks across multiple domains. We hypothesize that increasing model depth allows for better multi-modal behavior modeling, which is essential for in-context learning in complex, unstructured action spaces.
CONTROLS: We will train and evaluate DPT with depth as a hyperparameter, with competing models including a model with the standard 10-layered architecture, a state-of-the-art pretraining schedule for comparison, and AD as an ablation. We will also investigate the effect of intermediate layers for different layers alignments.
COST: 270 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that larger DPT models will provide improved performance on tasks that require nuanced action distributions, such as robot manipulation and humanoid control tasks. This could fail due to overfitting or increased risk of catastrophic forgetting with deeper network architectures, particularly when training them from scratch.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Task-Agnostic Exploration Policies via Robust Optimization for DPT
PROPOSAL: We will leverage robust optimization techniques to derive task-agnostic exploration policies for DPT, which can adapt to unseen tasks without requiring retraining. By leveraging the robustness of DPT as a posterior sampling-based model, we will develop a mathematical framework for deriving exploration policies that generalize across tasks and environments, enabling seamless adaptation to new domains.
CONTROLS: We will compare our task-agnostic exploration policies to state-of-the-art exploration policies and ablate the effect of the robust optimization framework by comparing it to a naive baseline. We will also evaluate the policies on a variety of tasks from the robotics and control domains.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our task-agnostic exploration policies are expected to provide improved adaptation and exploration capabilities on unseen tasks, as they are designed to be robust across multiple tasks and environments. However, the performance may suffer if the policies rely too heavily on robustness, potentially leading to over-conservatism or inefficient exploration.

TITLE: A Theoretical Analysis of the Generalization Properties of DPT
PROPOSAL: We will provide a theoretical analysis of the generalization properties of DPT, focusing on the effects of the posterior sampling objective on the model's ability to generalize to unseen tasks and environments. By leveraging tools from differential geometry and topological data analysis, we will derive bounds on the model's generalization error and investigate the role of task complexity and model capacity on generalization.
CONTROLS: We will compare our theoretical analysis to empirical results and ablate the effect of different objectives and model capacities on generalization.

TITLE: Learning to Adapt to Changing Task Rewards using a Novel Meta-Reinforcement Learning Objective
PROPOSAL: We will introduce a novel meta-reinforcement learning objective that enables DPT to adapt to changing task rewards and uncertainties. By incorporating a probabilistic representation of the reward function, our meta-RL objective will allow DPT to learn a robust policy that can generalize to a wide range of tasks and environments, even when the reward signals are uncertain or changing.
CONTROLS: We will compare our novel meta-RL objective to state-of-the-art meta-RL methods and ablate the effect of different components, such as reward uncertainty and probabilistic reward representations.

PREDICTION: Our novel meta-RL objective is expected to improve DPT's ability to adapt to changing task rewards and uncertainties, enabling more robust and generalizable policies. ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Robust Policy Transfer via Knowledge Distillation for DPT
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of knowledge distillation as a means to transfer policies from a high-capacity DPT model to a smaller, more deployment-friendly policy. By leveraging the interpretability of DPT as posterior sampling, we will develop a novel distillation framework that focuses on transferring knowledge in the form of probability distributions over actions, enabling robust policies that generalize to new tasks and environments.
CONTROLS: We will compare our knowledge distillation framework to state-of-the-art policy transfer methods and ablate the effect of different distillation metrics and techniques.
COST: 933.12 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our knowledge distillation framework is expected to improve the robustness of policy transfer for DPT, enabling more effective deployment of policies in real-world settings. However, the distillation process may lose some of the original policy's performance, particularly if the distillation metric is not well-aligned with the task's objectives.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling Multi-Modal Continuous Action Posteriors in DPT
PROPOSAL: Investigate adapting the Decision Pretrained Transformer (DPT) to utilize a non-parametric action distribution, specifically a betanormal mixture model, to capture complex multi-modal continuous action posteriors. Train this variant, called DPT-MM, on the offline synthetic data set of 200 diverse simulated environments, each featuring 50 varied continuous-control tasks in the problem list.
CONTROLS: Vanilla DPT, a baseline with a single beta distribution over 1D continuous actions, and an ablation study where DPT-MM is restricted to tasks with only 2D or 3D action spaces.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: DPT-MM should improve upon Vanilla DPT by up to 30% in terms of unseen task performance, or else it may fail when confronted with environments requiring strict assumption of action modality, like tasks with a very high action noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward-Augmented Inference in DPT-MM
PROPOSAL: Introduce an auxiliary reward-guided model, the Reward Augmented Decision Transformer (RADT), that refines the decision of DPT-MM on the current state by predicting the next state and reward. RADT is trained jointly with DPT-MM on the synthetic dataset. This setup seeks to leverage rewards during real-time adaptation while preserving the agent's capability for in-context learning.
CONTROLS: DPT-MM on its own, and an ablation study omitting the reward component of RADT to verify its contribution to adapting to new tasks and environments.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: RADT should bring about substantial improvements (over 50%) in new task performance for RADT when compared to DPT-MM on its own, as the reward signal will help the model navigate until episodes in complex unseen tasks. However, it may struggle on environments that require strict adherence to visited state transitions, due to its forward-looking support component.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Model for Complex Environments
PROPOSAL: To better address increasingly complex and high-dimensional environments characterized by multiple nested control loops and stratified hierarchies, develop a hierarchical extension of DPT-MM, allowing for the decomposition of tasks into clusters of correlated variables according to their values and relevance to action outputs. Train this hierarchical variant, H-DPT-MM, on the offline synthetic dataset, using the same 200 diverse simulated environments for rigorous evaluation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Multimodal Action Modeling for DPT
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel action distribution model for DPT, leveraging a mixture of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and normalizing flows. This enables DPT to capture complex, multi-modal continuous action posteriors, allows actions to be sampled natively at inference time, and preserves the agent's interpretation as Bayesian posterior sampling. Specifically, we use a hierarchical architecture with multiple GMMs and learnable transformation for action dimensionalities.
CONTROLS: Vanilla DPT, single-Gaussian action model, and mixture-model ablations.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: The new action model will show improved performance on multimodal tasks, while requiring minimal modifications to the DPT architecture. In some cases, the benefits will rely on careful prior selection and hyperparameter tuning, where overly broad posteriors might overwhelm action prediction, limiting the model's ability to focus on the dominant modality.

TITLE: Mixture Continuous DPT (MCDPT) for Multi-Modal Robot Control
PROPOSAL: We scale up DPT to robot manipulation and locomotion by developing MCDPT, a variant of DPT that incorporates an Mixture Continuous Recurrent Neural Network (MCRNN) as the policy. This architecture captures complex continuous action posteriors and allows the agent to reason about various robot configurations and task constraint spaces in the robot manipulation and locomotion domains.
CONTROLS: DPT with discrete-action model, MCRNN ablations, and vanilla MCRNN with no posterior sampling
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: MCDPT is expected to outperform previous approaches in diverse, high-dimensional robot control tasks. However, in less complex robot control environments where action posteriors are quasi-discrete, the model performance may degrade slightly compared to discrete-action models, highlighting the value of utilizing a general action model across multiple domains.

PROPOSAL: We provide formal analysis and proofs of policy robustness for DPT under uncertainty or noise in the environment latency and variability in observed expert demonstrations, arguing that DPT's ability to interpret its actions through posterior sampling is conducive to robustness properties. More specifically, DPT's variance-optimal behavior and predictive-based evaluation allow the model's robustness to generalize into continuous state and action space domains, according to Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) formulation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalizing DPT to Partially-Observed Environments through Auto-Encoder Pretraining
PROPOSAL: We extend DPT to partially-observed environments by introducing an auto-encoder pretraining mechanism where the encoder is used to impute missing observations during training and inference. This approach leverages the encoder's ability to reconstruct observations from partial states, and the DPT model can seamlessly integrate the imputed information to maintain its on- and offline generalization capabilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Multimodal Action Modeling for DPT
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel action distribution model for DPT, leveraging a mixture of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and normalizing flows. This enables DPT to capture complex, multi-modal continuous action posteriors, allows actions to be sampled natively at inference time, and preserves the agent's interpretation as Bayesian posterior sampling. Specifically, we use a hierarchical architecture with multiple GMMs and learnable transformation for action dimensionalities.
CONTROLS: Vanilla DPT, single-Gaussian action model, and mixture-model ablations.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: The new action model will show improved performance on multimodal tasks, while requiring minimal modifications to the DPT architecture. In some cases, the benefits will rely on careful prior selection and hyperparameter tuning, where overly broad posteriors might overwhelm action prediction, limiting the model's ability to focus on the dominant modality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mixture Continuous DPT (MCDPT) for Multi-Modal Robot Control
PROPOSAL: We scale up DPT to robot manipulation and locomotion by developing MCDPT, a variant of DPT that incorporates an Mixture Continuous Recurrent Neural Network (MCRNN) as the policy. This architecture captures complex continuous action posteriors and allows the agent to reason about various robot configurations and task constraint spaces in the robot manipulation and locomotion domains.
CONTROLS: DPT with discrete-action model, MCRNN ablations, and vanilla MCRNN with no posterior sampling
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: MCDPT is expected to outperform previous approaches in diverse, high-dimensional robot control tasks. However, in less complex robot control environments where action posteriors are quasi-discrete, the model performance may degrade slightly compared to discrete-action models, highlighting the value of utilizing a general action model across multiple domains.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: MCDPT On- and Offline Pretraining and Few-Shot Adaptation
REVISED-COST: 3600 (revise down from the initial 9000)

We modify 2. Mixture Continuous DPT (MCDPT) for Multi-Modal Robot Control by pretraining the model on a range of robotic environments before fine-tuning on smaller datasets for specific tasks. This allows MCDPT to adapt quickly to novel settings, even when exposed only to limited data. Offline learning and a smaller model size result in lower computational costs.
